articles.title: Which OpenAPI Codegen Should You Choose in 2026? 🤔 openapi-typescript vs Hey API vs Orval vs Kubb v5 🔥
articles.description: Hoi hoi!  I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who loves TypeScript, OSS, and getting lost in forests...
articles.body_html:
Hoi hoi!

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who loves TypeScript, OSS, and getting lost in forests of generated code. 🌳

Six months ago, I compared four OpenAPI code generators in this article 👇

Which OpenAPI Codegen Should You Choose? openapi-typescript vs hey-api vs Orval vs Kubb
nyaomaru
nyaomaru
May 20

Which OpenAPI Codegen Should You Choose? openapi-typescript vs hey-api vs Orval vs Kubb

#typescript #openapi #frontend #webdev
62 reactions Comments 15 comments
18 min read

I chose Hey API.

I'm still using it in production, and I'm pretty happy with it.

But Kubb has changed a lot with v5! 🚀

Faster generation? Better clients? A new plugin architecture?

Oh no. Time to go back into the forest. 🌳🌳🌳

Let's see what has changed!

🎯 TL;DR

Library Why I would choose it
openapi-typescript Types with minimal generated code
Hey API Clean SDKs and comfortable DX
Orval Flexible client, query, and mock generation
Kubb v5 Extensible code generation with much-improved clients

I'm keeping Hey API in my existing projects.

But for my next project? Kubb looks quite tempting. 👀

🕰️ Six months later

Here are the versions I tested (Kubb plugins have their own versions) 👇

Library May 2026 November 2026
openapi-typescript 7.13.0 7.13.0
Hey API 0.96.1 0.99.0
Orval 8.8.1 8.48.0
Kubb 4.37.2 5.20.2

Kubb had a major architectural overhaul, while Hey API and Orval continued improving their existing ecosystems.

Let's see what that actually means for us.

🏎️ How fast are they now?

For this investigation, I generated a synthetic OpenAPI specification using drf-spectacular.

  • 1,200 operations
  • 484 component schemas
  • 51,878 lines
  • Approximately 1.28 MB

I reran the previous versions using this new specification.

All measurements below are from the same Ryzen 9 7900 machine running WSL2 and Node.js 26. Each result is the median of eight measured executions after one warm-up.

Types only

Generating 484 shared component schemas

Library Time Peak RSS (max)
openapi-typescript 438 ms 191 MiB
Hey API 527 ms 240 MiB
Orval 866 ms 145 MiB
Kubb 337 ms 156 MiB

Wait, Kubb?! 😳

Types + Fetch SDK

I benchmarked both old and current versions on the same synthetic schema and machine.

Library Old version Current version Reduction
Hey API 7,406 ms 1,329 ms 82.1%
Orval 3,457 ms 1,723 ms 50.2%
Kubb 6,236 ms 1,155 ms 81.5%

That's a massive improvement for both Hey API and Kubb.

openapi-typescript took 751 ms to generate the full operation types, but it uses a generic runtime client rather than generating an SDK for every endpoint, so I've kept it separate.

Generation scopes and output structures still differ, and these aren't measurements against the original production API.

Also, generation isn't everything. A single TypeScript compilation took approximately 2.44 seconds for Hey API and 3.80 seconds for Kubb.

Fast generation doesn't necessarily mean faster everything.

Still, impressive work! 🚀

🌳 How big is the forest?

Here's the generated output for the full specification.

Library Files Source size
openapi-typescript 1 1.45 MB
Hey API 16 1.78 MB
Orval 1,926 2.18 MB
Kubb 2,897 3.13 MB

A house, a small town, a forest, and a very ambitious forest.

openapi-typescript/
  types.ts

hey-api/
  types.gen.ts
  sdk.gen.ts
  client.gen.ts
  client/
  core/

orval/
  api.ts
  schemas/

kubb/
  clients/
  types/
  .kubb/

I still prefer Hey API's relatively compact structure.

But Kubb's distributed files aren't necessarily a bad thing. Smaller individual files can make generated code easier to navigate and review.

These are generated source sizes, by the way—not application bundle sizes.

🧑‍💻 Let's actually call an API

Suppose we have three endpoints 👇

GET  /users
GET  /users/{id}
POST /users

openapi-typescript

Using its official companion, openapi-fetch

const client = createClient<paths>({
  baseUrl: BASE_URL,
});

client.GET("/users", {
  params: { query: { limit: 2 } },
});

client.GET("/users/{id}", {
  params: { path: { id: "1" } },
});

client.POST("/users", {
  body: { id: "1", name: "Ada" },
});

No generated function for every endpoint.

Just typed URLs, HTTP methods, and a generic client.

Small. Simple. Useful. 👍

Hey API 

getUsers({
  query: { limit: 2 },
});

getUser({
  path: { id: "1" },
});

createUser({
  body: { id: "1", name: "Ada" },
});

This is one of the main reasons I chose Hey API.

I don't need to remember the argument order of 1,200 functions.

Just query, path, and body.

My little brain is happy. 😸🧠

Orval

With useNamedParameters: true

getUsers({ limit: 2 });

getUser({ id: "1" });

createUser({
  id: "1",
  name: "Ada",
});

Request options can be passed separately, and custom mutators allow you to centralize transport logic. 👍

Kubb v5 

getUsers({
  query: { limit: 2 },
});

getUser({
  path: { id: "1" },
});

createUser({
  body: { id: "1", name: "Ada" },
});

This looks familiar. 👀

Kubb now gives me the consistent request structure I like in Hey API.

One of my previous concerns is gone. 😸🚀

⚠️ What happens when things explode?

Let's say our API returns

  • 200: User[]
  • 400: { message: string }
  • 409: { conflict: string }

I like result-based error handling, but sometimes I also want exceptions.

More importantly, I want TypeScript to know which error I'm dealing with.

openapi-fetch 

const result = await list();

if (
  result.response.status === 400 &&
  result.error !== undefined &&
  "message" in result.error
) {
  console.log(result.error.message);
}

Hey API 

const result = await list();

if (
  result.response?.status === 400 &&
  result.error !== undefined &&
  "message" in result.error
) {
  console.log(result.error.message);
}

You get typed error responses, but checking the nested HTTP status alone doesn't narrow the error body.

Orval 

const result = await list();

if (result.status === 400) {
  console.log(result.data.message);
}

if (result.status === 409) {
  console.log(result.data.conflict);
}

Nice!

The top-level status acts as a discriminant. 😸

Kubb v5 

const result = await getUsers({
  throwOnError: false,
});

if (result.status === 400) {
  if ("message" in result.error) {
    console.log(result.error.message);
  }
}

Kubb also provides status-based narrowing. The additional guard handles the possible empty error body. 👍

To throw or not to throw

  • Hey API 
await getUsers({
  throwOnError: true,
});
  • Kubb 
await getUsers({
  throwOnError: true,
});

Hey API defaults to result-style HTTP errors in the tested SDK; Kubb defaults to throwing. Both let me choose.

Or, with Kubb

const users = await getUsers({
  throwOnError: false,
}).unwrap();

I particularly like this little .unwrap().

Give me the data or reject. Thank you very much!

There are still differences in what each client considers an error.

Behavior Hey API Kubb
Result-style HTTP errors ✅ ✅
Configurable throwing ✅ ✅
Status-discriminated result — ✅
.unwrap() — ✅
Network failure in nonthrowing mode Returned error in tests Rejected in tests

Nonthrowing HTTP mode doesn't mean nothing can throw!

🪝 What about TanStack Query?

All four have a way to integrate with TanStack Query.

// openapi-react-query
$api.queryOptions("get", "/users");

// Hey API
getUsersOptions();

// Orval
getGetUsersQueryOptions();

// Kubb
getUsersQueryOptions();

One interesting difference appeared in the runtime tests:

Library HTTP 400 in tested query configuration
openapi-react-query Rejects
Hey API Rejects
Orval Resolves by default
Kubb Rejects by default

TanStack Query needs a rejected promise to recognize a failed request.

For Orval's tested Fetch configuration, enabling override.fetch.forceSuccessResponse: true changes that behavior.

Not a deal-breaker. Just something worth configuring before your query happily reports that everything is fine while your API is on fire. 🔥

🤯 The enum problem, again

Remember those little enums that caused so much trouble last time?

They're back.

Consider these schema fragments:

BlankEnum:
  type: string
  enum: [""]

NullEnum:
  enum: [null]

Here's what happened:

Case openapi-typescript Hey API Orval Kubb
Empty-string enum (3.0 fixture) ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Null-only enum (3.1 fixture) ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅

Kubb's previous blank-enum issue is fixed! 🎉

Its v4 already handled the tested null-only case correctly, so that isn't a new v5 improvement.

Interestingly, Hey API still has a problem with the null-only enum.

type NullEnum = never;

Oops.

Adding type: 'null' fixes the TypeScript type, but the generated Zod validator can still accept unrelated values.

The verified workaround for this OpenAPI 3.1 case is:

NullEnum:
  type: "null"

Now we get the correct type and validator:

type NullEnum = null;

const zNullEnum = z.null();

There's also an existing upstream issue.

It's a specific edge case, not a general problem with nullable properties.
But this is why I test generated types instead of simply trusting them.

🛡️ Type safety at runtime

TypeScript is wonderful. Unfortunately, my backend doesn't care. 😹

All four default clients accepted invalid response data in my tests. With runtime validation, all four rejected it.

Library Validation
openapi-typescript Manual
Hey API Generated Zod
Orval Generated Zod
Kubb Generated Zod

Encoding and decoding

Kubb has another interesting feature: directional transformations.

const result = await postTimestamp({
  body: { at: new Date() },
});

const date: Date = result.data.at;

With inferred: 'codec' and a custom datetime printer, Kubb generated the ISO string ↔ Date transformations and integrated them into the client.

These are directional Zod transforms, not native bidirectional z.codec objects.

Less glue code. Happy cats. 🐈

Server-Sent Events

Both Hey API and Kubb handled typed SSE in my tests.

// Hey API
const { stream } = await heyEvents();

for await (const event of stream) {
  console.log(event.value);
}

// Kubb
const { stream } = await kubbEvents();

for await (const event of stream) {
  console.log(event.data.value);
}

Different wrappers, same typed streaming goodness.

🧰 The ecosystem

Feature openapi-typescript Hey API Orval Kubb
Fetch ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Axios — ✅ ✅ ✅
React Query ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
SWR — ✅ ✅ ✅
Zod generation — ✅ ✅ ✅
Faker / MSW — ✅ ✅ ✅
Native custom plugins — ✅ — ✅

These are official integrations and companions, not necessarily built-in features. Other extension mechanisms exist.

One correction from my previous comparison: Hey API also supports Faker, MSW, and SWR. I verified Faker/MSW behavior and SWR generation.

The ecosystems are getting crowded. In a good way! 😸

🏗️ Kubb v5: More than an OpenAPI generator?

This is where Kubb gets interesting.

OpenAPI
   ↓
Unified AST
   ↓
Plugins + Resolvers + Macros
   ↓
Generated code

Kubb v5 lets plugins share a normalized AST instead of independently parsing the specification.

But what does that actually give us?

Resolvers

Let's say my project requires an Api prefix and .model.ts filenames.

import { pluginTs, resolverTs } from '@kubb/plugin-ts';

pluginTs({
  resolver: {
    name(name) {
      return `Api${resolverTs.name(name)}`;
    },
    file: {
      baseName({ name, extname }) {
        return `${name}.model${extname}`;
      },
    },
  },
});

The result?

- GetUsersOptions
+ ApiGetUsersOptions

Even better, the Fetch plugin automatically imports the renamed type from the renamed file.

No regex magic. No broken imports. Strict TypeScript compilation passed.

Macros

I also tested removing descriptions from TypeScript output while preserving them in Zod output.

It worked. Each plugin can transform its own AST without affecting the others.

Kubb Kit and Registry

Kubb Kit lets developers build custom generators using the same infrastructure as official plugins.

And the Kubb Registry lets the community distribute extensions.

Kubb registry · Kubb

The list of Kubb extensions that the Kubb CLI, Kubb Studio and kubb.dev read. It is a set of static JSON documents under one base URL.

kubb.dev

Hey API also supports custom plugins, so extensibility isn't unique to Kubb.

But the combination of shared AST, resolvers, macros, and Kit makes Kubb particularly interesting for building a company-wide generation platform.

🤖 AI can grow a forest overnight

AI makes generating code faster. Keeping it consistent? Not so much.

Imagine five AI agents building five features, each inventing different API wrappers and error handling.

Congratulations! Five different forests. 🌳🌴🌲🎋🌵

Why keep telling AI the same rules when we can encode them into a shared generator?

Let AI help build the plugins. Let deterministic codegen enforce the conventions.

One shared plugin can serve ten projects instead of ten AI agents reinventing the same thing.

Maybe the best use of AI isn't generating more code. It's building better tools that generate code for us.

And that's exactly why Kubb's architecture caught my attention.

🌱 Maintaining the forest

I also tested how generated code changes when the API evolves.

Library Changed files Added / removed lines
openapi-typescript 1 +2 / −2
Hey API 3 +9 / −9
Orval 3 +14 / −14
Kubb 6 +59 / −59

These results are from renaming one operationId.

All four generated identical output with unchanged input, and breaking schema changes were caught by application type checks.

More files aren't necessarily worse. Just keep your forest under control! 🌳

🤝 Kubb Studio

Kubb also introduced Kubb Studio, a separate collaboration service.

Kubb Studio · Generate typed clients from your API spec

Generate TypeScript clients, TanStack Query hooks and Zod schemas from your API spec on your own machines. Review every change, then ship from CI. Start free.

kubb.studio

It offers UI-based plugin configuration, generated-file comments, and npm snapshots through GitHub Actions.

That could help frontend teams work against upcoming backend contracts before release.

I haven't tested it hands-on yet, but it's an interesting direction!

📓 Side by side

openapi-typescript Hey API Orval Kubb v5
Approach Types SDK Configurable generators Extensible generators
Request style Typed URL Named options Configurable Named options
Output Minimal Compact Configurable Distributed
Errors Result Result / Throw Status / Throw Result / Throw / Unwrap
Validation Manual Generated Generated Generated
Extensions Scripts / AST Plugins Transformers / hooks Kit / Resolvers / Macros

🚀 Back out of the forest

Six months ago, I chose Hey API. And I'm keeping it.

But Kubb v5 surprised me.

It's faster, its clients have improved, and its architecture offers something beyond a ready-made SDK.

In the AI era, I think shared development foundations matter more than ever.

For my next large frontend project, I'd love to give Kubb a try.

Six months ago, I wanted a smaller forest.

Now, I want to design how it grows.

Before AI plants another million trees. 🌳🤖

Thanks for reading! 🙌💚

articles.title: Benchmark LiteRT.js Without Confusing WebGPU with a Faster App
articles.description: A browser benchmark can produce an impressive number while measuring only the easiest part of the...
articles.body_html:
A browser benchmark can produce an impressive number while measuring only the easiest part of the experience. Timing one inference call can hide runtime loading, model transfer, compilation, initialization, output readback, and the work the surrounding interface must still perform.

For a feature used once during a form submission, those costs may matter more than its tenth inference. For a continuously running camera feature, repeated inference may dominate. The benchmark needs to match the interaction.

This walkthrough builds a small LiteRT.js harness that can request Wasm or WebGPU execution for the same model. It records the phases separately, preserves raw samples, and keeps backend configuration distinct from user-perceived speed. It does not assume that requesting the GPU means every operation ran there, or that a result from one machine predicts every device.

Fix the workload before changing the accelerator

The companion pins @litertjs/core to 2.6.0 and downloads Google’s MobileNetV2 demo model. The downloaded file is 14,020,256 bytes. Its SHA-256 is recorded in the supplied model manifest, so someone repeating the experiment can verify that the weights have not changed.

The harness uses one deterministic floating-point tensor. That makes the input identical across accelerator runs and avoids including image decoding in an inference-only measurement. It is deliberately not an image-recognition accuracy benchmark.

For a product evaluation, add a separate dataset of licensed images and a verified preprocessing pipeline. A model can return finite numbers for incorrectly normalized input. Output shape and absence of exceptions are useful smoke checks, not evidence that the classifier understands the images.

Keep initialization visible

LiteRT.js separates loading its runtime from loading and compiling a model. Fetch the model explicitly when you want its transfer time to remain visible.

await loadLiteRt("/wasm/");
const response = await fetch("/model.tflite");
if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Model download failed.");
const bytes = new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer());
const model = await loadAndCompile(bytes, { accelerator });

The complete harness timestamps each phase and hashes the downloaded bytes outside the compilation interval. It reads the model’s input details rather than silently assuming a tensor layout. The example rejects models that do not have a single float32 input.

The supplied preparation command copies the runtime assets from the installed package. This keeps the JavaScript and Wasm versions aligned. Loading JavaScript from one release and Wasm from an unversioned CDN URL would introduce an avoidable variable.

Figure 1. Change the execution request while keeping the model and input fixed.

Include output readback in the timed operation

The example measures a result that JavaScript can actually inspect:

const start = performance.now();
const outputs = await model.run(input);
try {
  const data = await outputs[0].data();
  for (let i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
    if (!Number.isFinite(Number(data[i]))) {
      throw new Error("Non-finite output.");
    }
  }
  return performance.now() - start;
} finally {
  outputs.forEach(output => output.delete());
}

Output transfer can matter when comparing an accelerator with CPU execution. If you exclude it, label the metric accordingly and explain why the application can avoid that transfer.

Release input tensors and the compiled model after the benchmark as well. Otherwise, repeated experiments can accumulate resources and change the environment you think you are holding constant.

Separate the first run from the warm runs

The harness records the first inference, performs three additional warmups, then retains ten measured samples. It reports the median without discarding the underlying observations.

Recorded value Question it helps answer
Runtime load time How long did runtime initialization take?
Model fetch time and bytes What did obtaining the weights cost?
Compilation time What did preparing this backend cost?
First inference What happens before the runtime is warm?
Ten warm samples How variable is repeated execution here?
Output sample and length Did both runs produce comparable numerical output?

Ten samples are enough to inspect the harness, not to make a strong population-level tail-latency claim. Repeat whole sessions, alternate backend order, and report device conditions before drawing a performance conclusion.

Reload the page between accelerators. A reload resets the page’s runtime but does not necessarily clear the HTTP cache, operating-system caches, or driver caches. Describe the cache condition rather than calling every reload a cold start.

Check what WebGPU actually means in the run

The WebGPU branch first requests an adapter. If none is returned, it records an unsupported result instead of inventing a zero-duration measurement or quietly labeling a Wasm run as GPU execution.

LiteRT’s documentation notes that unsupported accelerated operations can fall back to CPU. Therefore, the requested accelerator is configuration evidence, not a complete execution profile. Capture available adapter information and use runtime diagnostics when making claims about where computation occurred.

A software adapter in a headless environment is also a different subject from a physical laptop GPU. Keep that distinction in the results table.

Run and interpret the experiment

From the companion’s lab directory, run npm ci, npm run prepare:model, and npm run build. Start npm run preview, open /benchmark.html, and run one accelerator per reload. Preserve the JSON output from each run with the browser and machine details.

The Wasm harness completed in Headless Chrome 153 on a virtualized Linux host: it accepted a [1, 3, 224, 224] input and returned 1,000 finite values through the first run, warmups, and ten measured runs. The raw JSON is included as an execution check. GPU execution was disabled in that environment, so these observations establish no WebGPU-versus-Wasm speed ranking. Hardware runs and an application-level responsiveness measurement remain necessary before recommending a backend for a real feature.

For the latter, measure an actual interaction while inference runs: typing into a field, opening a panel, or scrolling through results. A fast model invocation can coexist with a poor page experience if preprocessing or rendering blocks the main thread.

Which cost dominates your feature: obtaining the first useful answer, repeatedly processing frames, or keeping the surrounding interface responsive?

References

  • LiteRT.js overview and execution
  • LiteRT.js getting started
  • Client-side AI performance
  • Model caching guidance

articles.title: November's worst CVEs weren't clever. They were bad assumptions about state.
articles.description: If you only skim the headlines, November 2026 looks like a month of exotic exploits. Java4Shell....
articles.body_html:
If you only skim the headlines, November 2026 looks like a month of exotic exploits. Java4Shell. phpAfterShell. A Drupal bug with a name. Read the advisories instead and a less exciting picture shows up: most of the scariest bugs come down to code trusting a piece of state it never actually checked.

The advisory vs. the root cause

Advisories tell you what to patch. They rarely tell you what kind of mistake you are probably also making in your own code. The first part is urgent. The second part is the one that keeps paying off.

Here's the month in one list, then the patterns underneath it.

  • PHP (Nov 19): around 17 flaws patched, several of them critical RCEs rated CVSS 9.2. Includes phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714) and a PHP-FPM request-smuggling bug (CVE-2026-129289). This follows October's PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619). Fixed in 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36.
  • Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): pre-auth RCE in Java/JDK deployments. CISA issued an alert on Nov 17 after public PoCs spread across GitHub.
  • Drupal "Fail2Install" (CVE-2026-132165): pre-auth RCE, CVSS 9.8, core 8.9 through 11. Exploited in the wild and added to CISA's KEV catalog.
  • VMware vCenter (CVE-2026-123890): unauthenticated auth bypass, exploited for months by a suspected China-nexus espionage group before it reached KEV.
  • Cisco Expressway (CVE-2026-76466): unauthenticated command injection as root on clustered Expressway-C and Expressway-E.
  • Project MONAI Label (CVE-2026-133968): path traversal, added to KEV on Nov 23.
  • Microsoft Patch Tuesday (Nov 10): critical pre-auth RCEs in Windows Schannel and Exchange/Windows Search, plus an exploited Outlook spoofing zero-day (CVE-2026-124194) that leaks NTLMv2 hashes.

Failure mode 1: treating an error as a state

Fail2Install is the cleanest example of the month. The attacker exhausts database connections or file descriptors. Drupal's installer sees the failure and concludes the site is unconfigured. The attacker walks through setup and runs arbitrary PHP.

"I couldn't connect" and "there is no configuration" are two different facts. The code collapsed them into one.

Here's an illustrative version of the same mistake, the kind that shows up in plenty of apps:

function isInstalled(PDO $db): bool {
    try {
        return (bool) $db->query("SELECT 1 FROM settings LIMIT 1");
    } catch (Exception $e) {
        return false; // DB down? Table missing? Both become "not installed".
    }
}

The fix has two parts. Separate "absent" from "unknown" and fail closed on unknown. Then stop deriving "installed" from a runtime resource at all: write a marker at install time, and disable the installer route in production.

Failure mode 2: writes that aren't atomic

phpAfterShell comes from non-atomic session file writes. Between "file opened" and "file fully written" there is a window where another request can see, or shape, half-written state.

Most of us have written this:

with open(path, "w") as f:
    f.write(serialize(data))

The safer shape is to write to a temp file in the same directory, flush it, then rename it over the target. On POSIX filesystems the rename is atomic. The partial write never is.

Failure mode 3: two parsers, one request

The PHP-FPM smuggling bug (CVE-2026-129289) is the classic version of this. A proxy and a backend disagree on where one request ends and the next begins, and the attacker lives in the gap.

Any time two components parse the same bytes, the security boundary sits between their interpretations. Normalize at the edge. When a request is ambiguous, reject it instead of guessing.

Failure mode 4: input that becomes a path or a command

MONAI Label's path traversal and Expressway's command injection are the oldest bug classes on the list, still shipping in 2026. Resolve the path first, then check it's still under the root. Pass arguments as arrays, never as a shell string.

Failure mode 5: the box nobody owns

vCenter was exploited for months before anyone added it to KEV. Expressway sits at the network edge. Your app code can be spotless while the hypervisor console is wide open. An accurate inventory is a security control, not paperwork.

The reframe

Most of November's critical CVEs are state-management bugs with an RCE bolted on the end. The exploit is the last step. The mistake happened earlier, in an assumption about what "failed", "written", "ended" or "inside" means.

Patch first, then grep

Patch from the list above. Then spend an hour searching your own codebase for the same shapes: catch blocks that return "not configured", direct writes to shared files, path joins on user input, anything that builds a shell command from a string.

Which of these patterns have you actually found in your own code, and what caught it: review, tooling, or an incident?

articles.title: Remotion vs. CoAnimator When Your Product Demo Needs an Update
articles.description: You publish a product demo on Friday. On Monday, the Save button moves into an overflow menu.  You...
articles.body_html:
You publish a product demo on Friday. On Monday, the Save button moves into an overflow menu.

You replace the recording. Now the caption appears before the click, the voiceover describes the old UI, and the next scene starts too soon. Someone has to fix all three before the video can go live again.

That’s the edit I’d use to compare Remotion and CoAnimator. Both can work with coding agents. What matters after launch is whether the person who owns the video can make the change, review it, and verify the new export.

What you edit in each tool

Remotion uses React components and props

In Remotion, the composition defines how the video looks and changes over time. Props can hold details that vary between exports, such as a release title, screenshot, or translated caption. If you expose those details as inputs, the next release can reuse the composition without a code change. Remotion’s guide to parameterized videos

The Remotion team’s Agent Skills demo shows one example of a video made with this workflow.

CoAnimator uses editable scenes and a visual timeline

CoAnimator gives you a desktop editor with a stage and timeline. You can ask a coding agent to revise a scene, then inspect the footage, captions, and timing in the editor. That’s useful when the person approving the edit needs to see exactly where it lands in the video. CoAnimator documentation

This showcase gives you a view of the editor around the animation. Use the revision tests below to judge how it fits your own project.

A small Remotion composition you can render

In an existing Remotion starter project, save this as src/release-title.tsx. It registers its own composition and can be passed directly to the render command.

import {
  AbsoluteFill,
  Composition,
  interpolate,
  registerRoot,
  useCurrentFrame,
  useVideoConfig,
} from 'remotion';

type ReleaseTitleProps = {title: string};

function ReleaseTitle({title}: ReleaseTitleProps) {
  const frame = useCurrentFrame();
  const {fps} = useVideoConfig();

  const opacity = interpolate(frame, [0, fps], [0, 1], {
    extrapolateRight: 'clamp',
  });

  return (
    <AbsoluteFill
      style={{
        alignItems: 'center',
        justifyContent: 'center',
        padding: 96,
        backgroundColor: '#ffffff',
        color: '#172554',
        fontSize: 80,
        textAlign: 'center',
        opacity,
      }}
    >
      {title}
    </AbsoluteFill>
  );
}

function Root() {
  return (
    <Composition
      id="ReleaseTitle"
      component={ReleaseTitle}
      durationInFrames={90}
      fps={30}
      width={1920}
      height={1080}
      defaultProps={{title: 'Version 2.4 is live'}}
    />
  );
}

registerRoot(Root);

Render the default title, then pass in a new title and render again:

npx remotion render src/release-title.tsx ReleaseTitle out/v24.mp4

npx remotion render src/release-title.tsx ReleaseTitle out/v25.mp4 \
  --props='{"title":"Version 2.5 adds saved filters and shared views"}'

Watch both exports. The title changes and the fade stays the same. This is the smallest version of a changelog workflow where release data changes more often than the layout. Remotion render command

Three edits to run in both tools

Build the same short demo in each tool using the same recording, captions, and closing card. Save a baseline export before making changes. Then run these edits separately so you can tell where the work accumulates.

1. Change the title and screenshot

In Remotion, expose the title and screenshot as props and rerender with new inputs. In CoAnimator, open the matching scene in the timeline and update the title and image, or ask the agent to make those two changes.

Use a long title and a screenshot with a different aspect ratio. Check both MP4s for text overflow and poor cropping. If a routine copy change needs a manual layout adjustment, count that time.

2. Replace footage after the interface changes

In Remotion, replace the clip in the composition and update the cue frames for the caption and callout. In CoAnimator, swap the clip in the timeline and move those cues, or give the agent a request with a clear boundary:

Replace the recording in scene 2 with overflow-menu.mp4.
Show the menu opening before highlighting Save.
Move the caption to match the click.
Keep the intro and closing card unchanged.

Use the same replacement clip in both tools. Replay a few seconds on either side of the edit and check the narration, caption timing, and transition. If you use Git, the diff can show which files changed. Playback tells you whether those changes work together.

3. Update a closing card across 20 videos

In Remotion, put the card in a shared component and feed its URL from a common setting. Update that setting and rerender each video with its own inputs.

In CoAnimator, check whether your projects reference a shared card or contain separate copies. Apply the change to the shared source or update the copies, then export through the app or CLI.

Record how many files needed edits and how many exports you had to check. A scripted render helps with the export step. Whether the URL change takes one edit or twenty depends on how the projects share that card.

Rendering and licensing

Remotion CoAnimator
Render options Local CLI, server-side rendering, or AWS Lambda Local app and scripted exports through coa
Free option Eligible individuals and organizations with up to three people 720p local exports with a watermark
Paid option Creators at $25 per seat per month, or Automators at $0.01 per render with a $100 monthly minimum One-time license listed at $299 as a limited-time offer, with watermark-free exports up to 4K

Compare the license and the cost of running the workflow. Cloud compute and storage can add to a Remotion bill. With CoAnimator, include the machines you use to render and any external agent or media services. Remotion pricing · CoAnimator pricing

The handoff test I’d use to decide

Give the project and the replacement footage to the person who will maintain the demo. Ask them to make the revision and verify the new MP4 on a second machine. Record the time from receiving the footage to approving the export, including any missing assets, setup work, or requests for help.

I’d start with Remotion if most revisions are changes to data in a stable layout. I’d try CoAnimator if most revisions involve footage and timing that someone needs to review in a visual timeline. A team producing both automated changelogs and individually edited demos may use a different workflow for each.

FAQ

Can CoAnimator replace Remotion?

It can cover demos, tutorials, and launch videos that someone edits as individual projects. If your app builds many videos from customer data, Remotion’s props and rendering APIs give you a direct way to implement that workflow.

Can I use Remotion commercially on the free license?

Yes, if you meet the eligibility terms for individuals or organizations with up to three people. Remotion license and pricing

Can both tools render from a script?

Yes. Remotion offers a CLI and Node.js APIs. CoAnimator offers the coa CLI. Run a test export on the machine that will render your real projects, using the same fonts, footage, and output settings.

Which part takes your team longer after a release: making the edit or verifying the new export?

articles.title: The Internet Wasn't Built for Agents: The 30-Year-Old Assumption That's Breaking Everything
articles.description: In the space of five days this month, it felt like the whole internet flinched.  November 12 to 17,...
articles.body_html:
In the space of five days this month, it felt like the whole internet flinched.

November 12 to 17, 2026. Different causes, no proven link. That's the unsettling part. I'm not claiming those outages are connected. But they point at something I can't stop thinking about.

The internet has a second kind of user now: AI agents that browse, buy, send email and call APIs for us. Attackers have them too. Last week Google said attackers are already using AI agents to find and exploit software flaws automatically. Every day is starting to feel like a zero day.

Under all of it sits one assumption, made about 30 years ago, that agents quietly break. No patch fixes it.

This is the first post in a series on what I call Web 4.0, the agentic internet: what's broken, what I think comes next, and where I'm starting.

🧱 The One Assumption Behind the Whole Internet

For about 30 years we've built the internet around humans clicking buttons. Websites, apps, dashboards, forms and even most APIs assume a person kicked things off.

You can see it in the identity layer. Each piece identifies something specific:

- IP addresses: identify network interfaces.
- DNS: identifies domains.
- OAuth: authenticates users.
- API keys: identify applications.

None of them identifies an autonomous actor. So none of them can answer the questions that matter once an agent shows up at your door:

  • Who owns this agent?
  • What is it allowed to do?
  • Can another agent trust it?
  • Has it earned a good reputation?

Today, an agent borrows your cookies, your OAuth token or an API key someone pasted into a config file, and the server on the other side sees.. You.
It has no way to tell you apart from the agent acting in your name.

Note: if your security model can't tell a person from their agent, it can't limit either one.

💥 Seven Ways the Internet Breaks

The assumption that a human is behind every action runs through almost every layer of the web. Below are the seven places where I expect it to fail first as agents scale.

  1. Identity. An agent using your cookies looks exactly like you. The server can't tell the difference, so it can't treat them differently.
  2. Delegation. There's no standard way to give a machine scoped, revocable authority. You hand over a key and hope.
  3. Trust. Star ratings and reviews are easy for an agent to fake at scale. They were designed for humans who can only post so fast.
  4. Payments. Checkout flows assume a person making a conscious decision. "Click to confirm" means nothing when nobody is looking at the button.
  5. Interfaces. Agents scrape pixels that were made for eyeballs. Half of today's agent tooling is software squinting at a screen.
  6. Liability. When an agent causes harm, who answers for it: the user, the company that built the agent, or the model provider?
  7. Persistence. An agent has nowhere to live. It has no stable address, no home, no history that follows it around.

Each of these is a problem on its own. Together, they show that we're running a new class of actor on infrastructure that was never designed to recognise it.

🏙️ From Documents to Actors

The old internet is a library. You visit, you request a page, it renders, you read:

Request → Render → Read

The agentic internet looks more like a city. Things in it act, negotiate and settle on your behalf:

Intent → Negotiation → Action → Settlement

In the library you're a visitor. In the city, you're an owner.

To make that work, I think we need a few new building blocks. These are working names, and I expect them to change as the series goes on.

🌐 My Proposal: The Agentic Internet

Here's what I think the next layer of the internet should look like. It rests on a few new building blocks: Creators who own things, Worlds they control, Constructs that live and act inside those worlds, and Stewards that guard the borders between them.

These are working names, and I expect them to change as the series goes on.

My sketch of the agentic internet. Circles are Worlds, shapes inside them are Constructs, black triangles are Stewards, and the lines are permissioned channels that cross world boundaries.

Creators

The humans (or organisations) who own things and are ultimately responsible for them. Everything else in the model traces back to a Creator.

Worlds

Every Creator gets a sovereign, addressable space. It's more than a website; it's a world. One space replaces the 40 platform accounts you currently have scattered around the internet.

  • One address. A single, persistent identity others can find and connect to, with no platform in the middle.
  • Border control. You decide who enters, what they can do, and for how long. Access is negotiated, not assumed.
  • Composable. Worlds can host, hire and transact with things from other worlds.

Constructs

The one primitive, all the way down. An agent, an asset, an account, a storefront: each is a construct, and they all share one schema. A construct is a signed, addressable entity with identity, state, behaviour, authority and a history of receipts.

Here's the recursive bit I like: a World is just a construct that contains other constructs.

Stewards

This is where it gets spicy. I think the browser dies, and your Steward replaces it.

A Steward is an agent that represents you, guards your world's border and negotiates with everyone else's Stewards. The flow looks like this:

  1. You state intent: "Find me a supplier. Negotiate under these terms."
  2. The Steward executes. It negotiates, verifies and acts under the authority you gave it.
  3. You revoke whenever you want. Authority is scoped and revocable, so you stay in control.

The Six Primitives

Every construct needs to answer six questions:

Primitive The question it answers
Identity and behaviour Who are you?
Ownership Who owns you and what you produce?
Authority What are you allowed to do?
Settlement How do you pay and get paid?
Reputation Can I trust you?
History What have you done, on the record?

If the internet can answer those six for every actor, human or machine, most of the seven breaks above start to close.

💸 The Agentic Economy

Zoom out and you get an economy where agents are economic citizens. They discover services, negotiate, buy and settle on behalf of people. They hold budgets, earn money, and hire other agents.

Three numbers sum up how I think about it:

  • 1B humans directing. Each person runs a small fleet of agents carrying out their intent.
  • 1T agents operating. Autonomous actors transacting, hiring and earning, around the clock.
  • 0 counterfeit reputation. A forked or copied agent starts at zero. Trust comes from verifiable history, not star ratings. That last one matters most to me. With a trillion actors, reputation that can be copied or faked is worse than no reputation at all.

🤔 "Why Not Just Use MCP and A2A?"

Fair question, and I get it at every talk.

The current protocols are good. They each solve one layer well:

  • MCP gives agents tools.
  • A2A gives agents a way to talk to each other.
  • AP2 and friends start to cover agent payments.
  • Web Bot Auth (an IETF effort) lets an agent sign its requests so a site knows who it is.
  • Blockchain can give agents shared, verifiable trust and settlement. The gap is that nothing joins them. Each piece was designed on its own, so the seams between them are where things leak. An agent can prove who it is to a website, but not what it's allowed to do there. It can call a tool, but the tool can't tell which human the request came from, or whether that human has since changed their mind.

I don't think you fix that by gluing more pieces on. The pieces need to grow from the same primitive from day one. That's what Constructs are meant to be.

Pro Tip: when someone says "we already have a protocol for that", ask which question it answers. Usually it's one of the six, never all of them.

🧪 What I'm Still Not Sure About

I'd be lying if I said this was all figured out. Here are the questions I keep coming back to, and I'd love pushback on any of them:

  • Prompt injection. A Steward guarding your border still has to read content from strangers. Protocols can limit what a tricked agent is allowed to do, but they can't stop the trick itself. That part is a model problem.
  • Fake swarms. "Forked agents start at zero" stops copied reputation. It doesn't stop someone spinning up 10,000 fresh agents. Creating an identity probably has to cost something.
  • Blockchain at a trillion agents. I believe a neutral, verifiable trust layer matters. I'm less sure every action should touch a chain, given fees, latency and privacy. My current bet is off-chain receipts with on-chain anchors.
  • Adoption. Protocols win by being used, not by being clever. Big players are already writing standards for agent identity and payments, and this has to work alongside them.

🛠️ What Comes Next

Talking about a new internet is the easy part. So I'm turning this into actual protocols, starting small.

I mapped out 18 gaps where today's internet breaks for agents and grouped them into seven protocols. The first one I'm building is P2: Authority and Delegation. It answers one question: what is this agent allowed to do, for whom, and until when? It also lets you take that permission back everywhere at once.

I picked it first because it's the gap causing real damage right now (hello, stolen OAuth tokens). It can also build on standards that already exist instead of reinventing them.

Coming up in this series:

  1. The gap catalog: all 18 ways the internet breaks for agents.
  2. P2 explained: grants, delegation chains and one-click revocation.
  3. A working demo: a Steward giving a sub-agent scoped, revocable access across two services, then pulling the plug.

🏁 Final Thoughts

The document web made information free. The agentic internet makes action free.

We built the internet to connect information. Then we evolved it to connect people. Now we have to design it to connect intelligence, and to make sure the people stay in charge when we do.

A billion humans directing a trillion agents. Intent becomes execution, and trust becomes verification.

So here's my question for you: what would you build on an internet where machines act, and where you own the ground they stand on? Tell me in the comments.

🌠 If this resonates, follow along for the next parts, and let's connect on LinkedIn or at ukeme.us.

articles.title: I Don't Need Your Permission
articles.description: Software engineers have got it tough right now. I look at senior jobs asking for more years of...
articles.body_html:
Software engineers have got it tough right now. I look at senior jobs asking for more years of experience than I’ve even been in software. Then I look at the entry-level work I’m seeing and it’s like, So you want me to teach AI how to do the job I’ve been trying to get?

Yeah. That sucks.

And when somebody says they’re afraid AI is going to take away their livelihood, I get it. That fear is 100% understandable. I’ve spent years learning to design and build software, and now part of the work available to me is teaching the very thing that could replace me how to do it.

Then I go to a dev site, click “Top,” and I swear eight out of ten articles are about AI. I go to another one. Same thing. Every. Single. One. Of. Them. It’s the nature of the beast right now.

So what am I going to do? Take a system I designed, teach AI how I want it built, and check whether it can follow that design consistently. I can use the same tools reshaping my job to better my own situation, and I get to make choices about how I use them. If my own hardware can handle the work, I’ll run it locally. If I need more compute than I have, I’ll decide whether that particular job is worth sending to the cloud.

Am I happy that the job market looks like this? No. Am I going to sit here and wait for it to look the way I wanted it to? No, no, no, baby girl.

When I ask, “Why can’t you adapt?” I’m asking myself that, too. And some days my answer is, “I’d really rather just have a job.”

Here’s where I get a little philosophical about it. XD

I am more than software. I am more than the cloud. I am more than my job.

I write songs. I make games. I have stories I want to tell. I still have to figure out how to pay my bills. I just don’t need the answer to that question to tell me who I am. I create stuff, and I’m figuring out how to make a living doing it.

I’ve had music on SoundCloud that was used to train AI. I haven’t heard it play one of my songs back note for note. I get why another musician might feel differently about their work being used. For me, it’s wild how fast it can pick up patterns that took me years to learn. I still think I can outperform it in creativity. Output per second? Yeah, it’s got me there. XD

And that speed changes who gets to make things. I can write a story, design a game around it, and build it. I can’t afford a whole team of modelers, texture artists, and animators. When I can, I want to hire artists. Today, if I can use AI to get a character into a build and hand the game to a friend to see if it’s fun, I don’t see anything unethical about doing that.

That’s what I mean when I say AI is turning things from service to creation. I could be the guy who loses a gig because a developer can generate a music track now. I could also be the guy who finally gets his game playable because he can make an asset he couldn’t afford to commission. Both of those guys are me. Of course people who make a living doing this work are worried. And of course the person who’s had a game idea for ten years is excited that they can finally try it.

Would I prefer AI to be more tame and regulated? Absolutely. Sometimes it feels like we bought a pressure washer and decided to do the dishes with it. And this is already bigger than artists and software engineers. The tech is out there at massive scale. We’re going to put it in a bunch of places, find out where it actually helps, and probably spend a few years wishing we’d left some things alone.

Kind of like smartphones. We put everything on them, and now some days I miss snapping a flip phone shut and being done.

Hello, T9.

Anyway, this was a real roundabout way to give myself permission to create. I could’ve been working on my game this whole time. XD

articles.title: TraitHub - Find people by what they're like, not only by what they do - Looking for early adopters
articles.description: Hi dev.to, it has been a while since I wrote here.  No, I didn't get stuck in Vim... :)  I believe...
articles.body_html:
Hi dev.to, it has been a while since I wrote here.

No, I didn't get stuck in Vim... :)

I believe the current networking ecosystem has a gap where we try to fit everything a person is into a job title, and that has a strict limitation. If you think about it, someone can be, like me, an engineer and a healthy-life enthusiast, and those two things are hard to fit together.

Here is where TraitHub comes into play.

So what is it?

The short version: you find people by what they're like, not only by what they do.

You pick a few traits that fit you, like curious, blunt or early riser. Then you say what you're open to, like mentoring, beta testing or co-founding something. TraitHub uses that to show you people you'd probably get along with, and small groups called ports where you can do something together.

By defining badges that uniquely describe you, it increases your changes to find like-minded people and collaborate more efficiently.

On your profile, besides adding your traits and open to badges, you can additionally describe yourself, add a short timeline about your background, and more.

Finding people

You can browse everyone and filter by the traits you care about. Each person's card shows what you have in common, which I find is a nicer way to start a conversation than a job title.

Ports

A port is a small space built around something people share. Could be early morning runs, could be a craft, could be a project.

Each port lists the traits it's looking for, and you can see right away how many of them you have. If it's an open port and you have enough of them, you're in. Invite-only ports are up to the owner and each user can ask a port owner for an invite if it feels the port is a fit.

Inside there are discussions, and there are asks. An ask is basically "can someone help me with this?" and it goes to the members who said they're open to that kind of thing. If none of the ports fit, you can start your own.

Highlights

This is the feed. You post what you're working on or what you need help with, and everyone can see it. You can also keep a highlight inside one of your ports if it's not for everyone.

For a glimpse into the next section, people can collaborate on the platform, which means more than one person is responsible for the final result. In other words, a highlight can have more than one author, and you can add up to 5 collaborators to it.

Collaborations

When you find someone you'd like to work with, you send them a short request from their page and say what it's about. If they accept, the two of you get a private conversation. If they don't, that's the end of it. No chasing, no awkward follow-ups.

Dashboard

Port invites and asks that match what you're open to end up here, so you don't have to go looking for them.

In addition, the latest comments on your posts, highlights and discussions you've bookmarked, your ports and how many people have traits related to your port, and many more end up here as well.

The favour

Each account created goes to a waiting list. We are letting people in a few at a time, so there's someone to meet when you show up. It's free.

If you can spare some time, use it and tell me what's confusing, what's broken, and what you wish it did. If you try it and think "why would I ever use this", feel free to tell me that in the comments. I'd much rather hear it now.

Sign up at https://traithub.com and we will be glad to let you in!

If you've reached this far, thank you for reading :)

P.S. It's built with .NET and Angular on Azure, if you're curious. Happy to talk about any of it in the comments.

articles.title: Before Switching to P2P, I Measured Whether WebRTC Would Even Connect
articles.description: I'm building Clipboard Share, a browser clipboard for moving files between devices on the same...
articles.body_html:
I'm building Clipboard Share, a browser clipboard for moving files between devices on the same network: https://www.clipboardapp.org. I wanted to make transfers faster by using WebRTC. Before changing anything, I shipped a small probe that only measures whether a direct connection works.

One thing up front: file transfer is still not P2P. Files go to Cloudflare R2 and the receiver downloads from R2. The only place in the codebase that creates a DataChannel is the probe, and it sends throwaway test data.

Why I looked at P2P

The current flow is "upload everything, then download." With a multi-GB file, the receiver waits for the whole upload even if the sender is sitting next to them. The goal in docs/p2p-decision.md:

When the other device is already in the room, send the file over WebRTC directly and cut the wait of "download only after the upload finishes."

Why measure first

Direct connections fail in some network setups, and a device that joins later can't receive anything over a connection that no longer exists. So the doc states a rule before any data came in:

Files are always stored in R2. P2P is only a faster path for devices that were already connected at send time. Devices that join later, or refresh, get the file from R2 as they do today.

It also fixes the pass criteria up front (dated 2026-10-24): C1 connection rate >= 85%, C2 transfer completion >= 97% with zero mismatches, C3 P2P median speed bucket at least one step above R2 uploads, C4 at least 30 uploads of 8 MB+ in 7 days. Miss any one and the next step doesn't happen. If it passes, the next step is a "shadow mode": keep uploading to R2 as usual, and have the receiver verify P2P data with SHA-256 per 1 MB, then discard it.

How the probe works

Nothing changes on screen. When a device joins a room that already has another device, it tries to connect and reports the result as a GA4 p2p_probe event.

1. The server only relays signaling

Offers, answers and ICE candidates travel over a Socket.IO event, p2p:signal. The handler forwards {to, data} as {from, data}, and only to a socket in the same IP room:

const ipRoomId = socket.ipRoomId;
if (!ipRoomId || to === socket.id) return;
const target = io.sockets.sockets.get(to) as ExtendedSocket | undefined;
if (!target || target.ipRoomId !== ipRoomId || !target.rooms.has(ipRoomId)) return;

target.emit('p2p:signal', { from: socket.id, data });

The only thing it checks about data is its size (16 KB cap after JSON serialization). There's also a per-socket token bucket (burst 40, 20/sec).

2. Classify how it connected

Once the channel opens, I read the selected candidate pair from getStats(). There's no TURN server, so a relay candidate counts as a failure.

export function classifyCandidateTypes(localType, remoteType) {
  const valid = ['host', 'srflx', 'prflx', 'relay']
  if (!valid.includes(localType) || !valid.includes(remoteType)) return 'failed'
  if (localType === 'relay' || remoteType === 'relay') return 'failed'
  if (localType === 'srflx' || remoteType === 'srflx') return 'direct_nat'
  return 'direct_lan' // host/prflx
}

3. Send test data and verify it

A connected channel can still be useless, so the probe actually sends data: 8 MB on a LAN path, 2 MB through NAT. Each 16 KB chunk starts with its index; the receiver only counts bytes and checks order, then drops the data.

export const PROBE_BYTES_LAN = 8 * 1024 * 1024
export const PROBE_BYTES_NAT = 2 * 1024 * 1024

// receiver: replies ack:<bytes>:<ok|bad> on the end signal
recvBytes += d?.byteLength ?? 0
if (readChunkIndex(d) !== expectIdx) orderOk = false
expectIdx++

The sender marks it complete only if the acked byte count matches and the order flag is ok; otherwise mismatch. The transfer timeout scales with size: max(8 s, bytes / 1.5 Mbit/s), capped at 30 s. If the connection itself isn't up in 8 seconds, it's failed.

4. Once per session, and it can't break the app 

export const SESSION_FLAG = 'p2p_probe_done'

export function isProbeEnabled(envValue = import.meta.env?.VITE_P2P_PROBE_ENABLED) {
  return envValue !== 'false'
}

One probe per session (sessionStorage), every exception is swallowed with a console.warn, and VITE_P2P_PROBE_ENABLED=false turns it off. The unit tests cover timeout to failed, mismatch on bad bytes or order, stalled when no ack arrives, and closed when the channel drops mid-transfer.

For comparison I also log real R2 upload speed: a successful upload of 8 MB or more sends an upload_perf event (upload_mbps, upload_path, retries, resumed, and so on). P2P only matters if it beats that.

Results

Between Oct 24 and Nov 25, GA4 recorded 672 p2p_probe events from 428 users. 177 of them came in the last 7 days, so the probe is still running.

What Count
Probes that got an answer from the peer (got_answer=true) 533
Direct connection direct_lan / direct_nat 394 / 39
Connection failed 238
Test transfer complete / stalled / other (closed, error, complete_legacy) 395 / 30 / 3
Data mismatch 0

Checked against the thresholds I wrote down first:

  • C1 connection rate: 433 direct ÷ 533 answered ≈ 81%. Below the 85% bar.
  • C2 transfer completion: 395 complete out of 428 test transfers ≈ 92%. Below the 97% bar. There were zero mismatches, so data never arrived wrong; most of the gap is stalled (no reply to the end signal).
  • C3 speed and C4 demand: the upload_perf event I use as the R2 baseline shows 0 events in GA4 for this period. I haven't found out why yet, so I can't judge speed or demand.

The rule was "if any check misses, don't move to the next step." With these numbers, shadow mode doesn't start.

What's still weak

  • One probe per session with 2-8 MB of data. It may not match a multi-GB transfer.
  • Results are GA4 aggregates, so I can't drill into which device pairs fail.
  • It only tries the first peer in the room (peers[0]), so a room with many devices is measured as one pair.
  • STUN only, no TURN. Networks that block direct connections simply count as failures.
  • There is no P2P file transfer code today. The criteria are written down, but the shadow-mode step and anything after it don't exist yet.

I built this with Claude Code. If you try it, I'd like to hear what's rough. There's a feedback link at the bottom of the site: https://www.clipboardapp.org

Originally published in Korean on velog.

articles.title: npm audit Found 69 Vulnerabilities in My Two SaaS Apps. Most of the Work Was Sorting Them.
articles.description: At Null Studio I write maintenance guides for clients. One of them, on what software costs after...
articles.body_html:
At Null Studio I write maintenance guides for clients. One of them, on what software costs after launch, splits upkeep into four kinds: corrective, adaptive, preventive and security. It ends with seven questions to settle before launch. The first one is "Who receives deprecation and security notices from each platform and service we use?"

I had never asked that about my own products. So this week I ran npm audit against the production branches of the two SaaS apps I run myself: VoiceDash (white-label client portals for Retell voice agents, Next.js + Prisma + Postgres) and Upwork Scout (AI-matched Upwork job alerts, Next.js + Firestore).

The headline numbers were not great.

voicedash   41 vulnerabilities (1 low, 13 moderate, 24 high, 3 critical)
gig-scout   28 vulnerabilities (16 moderate, 11 high, 1 critical)

69 advisories across two apps. Here is how I sorted them, what the tool got wrong, and the boring answer to the "who gets notified" question.

Step one: audit the lockfile you actually deploy

My local VoiceDash checkout was 37 commits behind main, so auditing it would have told me about code nobody runs. I pulled the deployed package.json and package-lock.json straight from the branch into a scratch folder and audited the lockfile alone, with no install:

git show origin/main:package.json > /tmp/vd/package.json
git show origin/main:package-lock.json > /tmp/vd/package-lock.json
cd /tmp/vd && npm audit --package-lock-only --json > audit.json

--package-lock-only is the useful flag here. It audits the exact tree Vercel installs, it is fast, and it does not run anyone's postinstall script on my machine.

Step two: drop dev tooling, then notice the filter lies

The obvious next move is --omit=dev, because a vulnerable ESLint plugin is not reachable from an HTTP request.

voicedash   41 -> 27 production advisories
gig-scout   28 -> 18 production advisories

That looked like progress until I mapped every remaining advisory back to the direct dependency that pulls it in. I wrote a small script that walks packages in the lockfile from each entry in dependencies and records which roots reach each vulnerable package. For VoiceDash:

Root dependency Production advisories it brings
prisma (the CLI) 15
next 6
next-auth 2
resend 3
zod 1

Fifteen of the 27 "production" advisories come through the Prisma CLI: hono, @hono/node-server, mysql2, chevrotain, lodash, effect and friends. My app does not serve requests with Hono and does not talk to MySQL. Those packages are there because the CLI ships a local dev server and schema tooling.

So why did --omit=dev keep them? Because prisma sits in dependencies, not devDependencies, in my own package.json. The scripts are "postinstall": "prisma generate" and "build": "prisma generate && next build", so the CLI has to be installed at build time, and at some point I put it in the production list. Vercel installs dev dependencies during the build anyway, so it could move. The audit filter trusts my package.json, and my package.json was wrong.

That does not make those 15 advisories irrelevant. Build tooling runs on a machine that holds my environment variables. It does mean they are a different risk from a bug in the request path, and they should not be ranked by npm's severity label alone.

Upwork Scout split cleanly by comparison: 11 of its 18 come through firebase-admin (gRPC, Google Cloud clients, fast-xml-parser, @fastify/busboy), 6 through next, and 1, zod, arrives only through the Anthropic SDK. The app itself does not import zod.

Step three: read the fix before running it

npm audit attaches a proposed fix to each advisory. Two of them would have hurt.

The firebase-admin "fix" is a downgrade. Upwork Scout runs firebase-admin 13.10.0. The advisory range is 11.0.0 - 14.3.0, and npm's suggested fix was:

"fixAvailable": { "name": "firebase-admin", "version": "12.1.0", "isSemVerMajor": true }

12.1.0 was published in April 2024. The current release is 14.5.1, which sits outside the vulnerable range. npm audit fix --force would have moved my app back two years and across a major boundary in the wrong direction. The real fix is a forward major upgrade that I need to test against my Firestore code, which is exactly the kind of adaptive work the client guide says to budget for.

prisma@latest is a release candidate. VoiceDash runs Prisma 7.5.0. The vulnerable range ends at 7.10.0, and 7.10.1 is the newest stable 7.x. But the latest dist-tag on npm currently points to 8.0.0-rc.35. If I had typed npm i prisma@latest to clear the warning, I would have shipped a release candidate of my ORM to production. The fix I want is prisma@7.10.1 and @prisma/client@7.10.1, pinned together.

The other two big ones were simpler. Both apps pin next to an exact version, which is the create-next-app default, so npm update never touches it. The patched release is in the same major. The auth library in VoiceDash is a beta release, and the patched build is a later beta of the same line. Those are the first two bumps, because they sit in front of every request.

The triage order I ended up with

  1. Request path, patch available in the same major: Next.js in both apps, the auth library in VoiceDash. Bump, build, click through login and one paid flow.
  2. Request path, needs a major: firebase-admin 13 to 14 in Upwork Scout. Read the changelog, run the scan endpoint against a test project, then ship.
  3. Build-time only: the Prisma CLI chain. Bump to 7.10.1 and move prisma to devDependencies so the next audit tells the truth.
  4. Transitive, waiting on a parent: zod via the Anthropic SDK, svix and uuid via Resend. These clear when the parent package updates, so they ride along with routine bumps.

I have not shipped any of this yet. This post is the audit, not the victory lap.

The answer to "who gets notified?"

Nobody. I checked both repos with the GitHub API:

gh api repos/<owner>/voicedash/dependabot/alerts
# "Dependabot alerts are disabled for this repository." (403)

Same response for Upwork Scout. Neither repo has a dependabot.yml or a Renovate config, and neither has a CI workflow that runs an audit. VoiceDash's only workflow pings Supabase so the free tier does not pause, and Upwork Scout's only workflow pings the scan endpoint every 15 minutes.

The git history tells the same story. Upwork Scout's package-lock.json last changed on July 7, two days after the first commit. VoiceDash's last changed on October 5, when I added a feature that needed it. Every dependency change in either repo happened because I was building something, never because I was maintaining something. In the guide's terms, I have been doing corrective work and zero preventive or security work, and the only reason I know is that I finally ran the command.

That pattern is familiar. I already wrote about a cron job that returns 200 when every fetch fails and about a model setting nobody re-checks. A missing notification channel is the same bug in a different place: the system is quiet, so it looks healthy.

What I am changing

  • Turn on Dependabot alerts for both repos, so security notices land in my inbox instead of waiting for me to remember.
  • A weekly audit job in CI that runs npm audit --package-lock-only --omit=dev --audit-level=high and fails loudly. Combined with step 3 above, the output will finally mean what it says.
  • Fix the dependencies list so build tools live in devDependencies.
  • Never run npm audit fix --force unread. Read fixAvailable, and if isSemVerMajor is true, check whether the suggested version is older than what you have.
  • Pin to a version, never to @latest, at least for anything that touches the database.

The takeaway

npm audit is a good smoke detector and a bad triage nurse. The raw count told me almost nothing. The useful information came from three questions the tool does not ask: does this package run in the request path, does the fix move me forward or backward, and who would have found out if I never ran the command?

How do you handle this on small products? Do you let Dependabot or Renovate open PRs automatically, or do you batch dependency work into a regular maintenance day?

This post is adapted from the client guide Software Maintenance After Launch on the Null Studio blog, held up against my own two apps.

articles.title: Turning YouTube caption files into clean text and SRT, and the four traps on the way 🧹
articles.description: Quotes encoded twice, tags inside lines, two kinds of English, and subtitles that talk over each...
articles.body_html:
Quotes encoded twice, tags inside lines, two kinds of English, and subtitles that talk over each other.

Hi! I'm Tim, a self-taught developer in Nairobi. I build small data tools that run as Apify Actors, serverless jobs that people pay for per result.

One of them turns YouTube videos into transcripts. Most people want those for AI tools: a chatbot over a channel, summaries, search. Some want subtitle files. Either way, the job ends with the same small problem: a caption file comes in, and clean text has to come out.

This post skips how you get the file and looks at what's inside it, because that's where the surprises are.

📄 The format

YouTube serves captions in several formats. The simplest is an XML format called srv1 (tools like yt-dlp can save captions in it too). It looks like this:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?>
<transcript>
  <text start="0.5" dur="2.1">It&#39;s &quot;fine&quot; &amp; good</text>
  <text start="2.6" dur="1.9">line
break <font color="#E5E5E5">here</font></text>
  <text start="4.5" dur="1">   </text>
  <text start="5.5" dur="2">café ’ok’</text>
</transcript>

One <text> per caption line, with a start time and a duration in seconds. Simple enough to parse with one regex. That small example holds three of the four traps.

🪤 Trap 1: the text is encoded twice

Look at the first line again: It&#39;s. That's an apostrophe encoded as ', and then the & of that encoded again as &.

Decode it once, the way any XML parser would, and you get:

It's "fine" & good

A parser that decodes once saves exactly that. It looks fine in a quick test, because most lines have no quotes, and then every "it's" and "don't" in a long transcript comes out as '.

The fix is to decode until the text stops changing:

const NAMED = { amp: '&', lt: '<', gt: '>', quot: '"', apos: "'", nbsp: ' ' };

function decodeOnce(s) {
    return s.replace(/&(#x[0-9a-f]+|#\d+|[a-z]+);/gi, (m, e) => {
        if (e[0] === '#') {
            const code = e[1] === 'x' || e[1] === 'X' ? parseInt(e.slice(2), 16) : parseInt(e.slice(1), 10);
            return Number.isFinite(code) && code > 0 && code < 0x110000 ? String.fromCodePoint(code) : m;
        }
        return NAMED[e.toLowerCase()] ?? m;
    });
}

// Caption text is often encoded twice (&#39;), so decode until it stops changing, at most 3 times.
export function decodeEntities(s) {
    let out = String(s ?? '');
    for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        const next = decodeOnce(out);
        if (next === out) break;
        out = next;
    }
    return out;
}

A few details that matter:

  • Numbers come in two forms. é is decimal and ’ is hex. Both have to work, and String.fromCodePoint handles characters outside the basic range, which fromCharCode gets wrong.
  • Unknown names stay as they are. &foo; isn't a real entity, so it's left alone instead of becoming an empty string.
  • The loop has a cap. &amp;lt; takes three passes to become <. Three is enough for what YouTube sends, and the cap stops a strange input from looping on.

There's a trade-off: if a caption genuinely contained the text <, it would be decoded too far. In speech captions that almost never happens, so I accepted it.

🪤 Trap 2: tags and line breaks inside a line

The second line has a line break in the middle and a <font> tag around one word. Caption text can carry styling like that, and none of it belongs in a transcript.

The whole line parser:

export function parseSrv1(xml) {
    const segments = [];
    const re = /<text\b([^>]*)>([\s\S]*?)<\/text>|<text\b([^>]*)\/>/g;
    let m;
    while ((m = re.exec(String(xml ?? '')))) {
        const attrs = m[1] ?? m[3] ?? '';
        const start = Number((attrs.match(/\bstart="([\d.]+)"/) || [])[1]);
        const duration = Number((attrs.match(/\bdur="([\d.]+)"/) || [])[1] ?? 0);
        const text = decodeEntities(m[2] ?? '')
            .replace(/<[^>]+>/g, '')   // drop styling tags
            .replace(/\s+/g, ' ')      // line breaks and runs of spaces become one space
            .trim();
        if (!Number.isFinite(start) || !text) continue;   // skip blank lines and broken ones
        segments.push({ start: round(start), duration: round(Number.isFinite(duration) ? duration : 0), text });
    }
    return segments;
}

const round = (n) => Math.round(n * 1000) / 1000;

Three things happen to every line:

  • Tags go, so <font color="#E5E5E5">here</font> becomes here.
  • Whitespace collapses, so line\nbreak becomes line break.
  • Empty lines are dropped. The third <text> in the example is only spaces. Keeping it would put an empty cue in the subtitle file.

The regex also accepts a self-closing <text ... />, which is an empty line written the short way.

Order matters here. Tags are stripped after decoding. That means an encoded < followed later by > in the same line would be decoded into something that looks like a tag and then removed. Captions of speech practically never contain that. If yours might, strip tags first and decode second.

From the example, the parser returns:

[
  { start: 0.5, duration: 2.1, text: 'It\'s "fine" & good' },
  { start: 2.6, duration: 1.9, text: 'line break here' },
  { start: 5.5, duration: 2,   text: 'café ’ok’' },
]

For AI tools I join those into one block of text. A 15-minute speech comes out at about 2,300 words, small enough to hand to a model whole. The segments stay in the output too, because timestamps are what let you link an answer back to the second it was said.

🪤 Trap 3: there's more than one English

A video usually has several caption tracks. Each has a language code, and YouTube marks the ones its speech recognition made: kind is "asr", or the track's vssId starts with a..

So "give me English" isn't one question, it's three:

  1. Which of the languages I asked for, in my order?
  2. Does en match en-GB?
  3. Should a written track beat an automatic one?

My rules:

export const isAuto = (track) => track?.kind === 'asr' || /^a\./.test(track?.vssId ?? '');
export const baseLanguage = (code) => String(code ?? '').toLowerCase().split(/[-_]/)[0];

export function pickTrack(tracks, { languages = ['en'], preferManual = true, fallbackToAny = true } = {}) {
    const list = (tracks ?? []).filter((t) => t?.baseUrl);
    if (!list.length) return null;
    for (const lang of languages) {
        const exact = (t) => String(t.languageCode ?? '').toLowerCase() === lang;
        const loose = (t) => baseLanguage(t.languageCode) === baseLanguage(lang);
        const candidates = [...list.filter(exact), ...list.filter((t) => !exact(t) && loose(t))];
        if (!candidates.length) continue;
        const manual = candidates.find((t) => !isAuto(t));
        const auto = candidates.find((t) => isAuto(t));
        return { track: preferManual ? (manual ?? auto) : (auto ?? manual), matched: true };
    }
    if (!fallbackToAny) return null;
    // Nothing matched: the automatic track is in the language actually spoken, so it's the best guess.
    return { track: list.find(isAuto) ?? list[0], matched: false };
}

My favourite test case: a video has Arabic, automatic English, British English written by a person, and Spanish. Asked for en, which wins?

// T(code, auto) builds a fake track for the test
const tracks = [T('ar'), T('en', true), T('en-GB'), T('es')];
pickTrack(tracks, { languages: ['en'] }).track.languageCode;   // 'en-GB'

The written en-GB beats the automatic en, even though en is the exact match. A person's captions have punctuation and fewer misheard words, and for a transcript that matters more than the region. If someone wants the automatic one, preferManual: false flips it.

When nothing matches, I return matched: false and say so in the output. Quietly handing back Arabic to someone who asked for English would look like a bug.

🪤 Trap 4: subtitles that talk over each other

An SRT file is the easy part, except for one thing. Each cue needs an end time, and start + duration doesn't always stop before the next line starts. When cues overlap, players show two lines stacked on top of each other.

So each end is clamped to the next start:

function srtTime(seconds) {
    const ms = Math.max(0, Math.round(seconds * 1000));
    const h = Math.floor(ms / 3_600_000);
    const m = Math.floor((ms % 3_600_000) / 60_000);
    const s = Math.floor((ms % 60_000) / 1000);
    const pad = (n, w = 2) => String(n).padStart(w, '0');
    return `${pad(h)}:${pad(m)}:${pad(s)},${pad(ms % 1000, 3)}`;
}

export function toSrt(segments) {
    return segments.map((s, i) => {
        const next = segments[i + 1];
        let end = s.start + (s.duration || 2);       // no duration: show it for 2 seconds
        if (next && end > next.start) end = next.start;
        return `${i + 1}\n${srtTime(s.start)} --> ${srtTime(end)}\n${s.text}\n`;
    }).join('\n');
}

Three cues, the first one too long, the second with no duration, the third an hour in:

1
00:00:00,500 --> 00:00:03,000
a

2
00:00:03,000 --> 00:00:05,000
b

3
01:01:01,250 --> 01:01:02,750
c

The first cue wanted to run until 5.5 seconds and was cut at 3.0, where the second starts. The second had no duration, so it got 2 seconds. And SRT wants a comma before the milliseconds, not a dot. A dot is WebVTT's style, and some players and editors won't read an SRT file that uses one.

✅ What I'd tell myself before starting

  • Test with a line that has an apostrophe in it. Double encoding hides until then.
  • Decode, strip tags, collapse whitespace, drop empties, and decide on purpose which order the first two go in.
  • Treat "which language" as a rule you write down, including what happens when nothing matches, and say so in the output.
  • Clamp subtitle end times to the next start, and use the comma.

All of these are pure functions with no network calls, so each one has a small unit test, the British English case included. Tests like that are cheap to write and they pin down the decisions, not just the parsing.

articles.title: When does a design decision become an architectural decision?
articles.description: Introduction   In the book "Fundamentals of Software Architecture", the authors define...
articles.body_html:
Introduction

In the book "Fundamentals of Software Architecture", the authors define software architecture like so:

« The software architecture of a system consists of an architecture style as the starting point, combined with the architecture characteristics it must support, the logical components to implement its behavior, and finally the architecture decisions justifying it all »

Four dimensions that architects must think about when conceiving the system. In our journey to explore what an architect must do and think, we'll start by talking about Architecture vs Design. When is a decision a design decision? When does it become an architectural decision?

What's the difference?

Imagine that you have an outdoor space that you want to transform into a garden. Your dream garden.

How many trees does it have? Does it have a barbecue set in concrete? Is it surrounded by hedges? Do you want to create a pond?

These decisions define the structure of your garden, that would be its architecture.

Now, let's get more detailed. Do you want to plant flowers? Which type? Are they red? Blue? What color should the barbecue be?

These are more about the design of your garden.
