Why is the pond architecture and the flower color design? Because removing a pond means digging up the garden, while changing flowers takes an afternoon.

The criteria

But how do you know for sure which is which? Well, like most things in software, it depends. Software architecture is all about context. Each context might make you choose different answers to a problem, and yet, each answer may be right.

There are three questions to ask ourselves:

  • Is it more strategic or more tactical? What's the scope?
  • How much effort does it take to implement or change? Meaning, not only doing the change, but what if I need to rollback the entire decision ?
  • How significant are the trade-offs? What are the compromises?

Asking yourself each of these questions will give you a pretty solid idea of which side of the spectrum your decision is.

Strategic vs tactical

How can we know if a decision is more of a strategic one or a tactical one?

Well, the book provides us with a few subjective questions. Things like:

  • how much thought and planning is involved in the decision?
  • how many people involved in the decision?
  • is it a long-term strategic decision or a short-term tactical one?

Let's take examples.

We have a module billing. A component that displays information wants to use the Observer pattern to refresh itself.

Architecture or design?

In this case, everything stays in the same module. It shouldn't affect a lot of people on the team so its scope is small. Design.

But what about: billing wants to react to the changes on the module users. Module maintained by another team and more modules plan on doing the same thing. Well now, that decision creates a contract between modules, and we have to coordinate with another team. Architecture

It's all about context. Both cases feel very similar, a module wants to use the observer pattern. But in the end, the decisions are completely different, yet both rankings are correct. It's not the technique or the person that determines the ranking, it's the impact of the decision.

Cost of Change

This one is pretty straightforward. How much time do I need to implement that change? What does it cost to do it? And also, NOT do it? Does it become more and more costly as time goes by?

For example, a developer chooses to store an amount field in float in the database. What seems like a simple type decision is actually on the architecture spectrum. If my whole application handles those amounts, everything is impacted. Plus, this decision is written in the database model so the cost becomes higher as time goes by, because every transaction persisted is more data we'll eventually have to migrate. And what if we decide to rollback that decision in 2 years? That is costly. All of this makes it fall on the architecture side of decisions.

Trade-offs

In software, we compromise. We have constraints to work with. Sometimes we have to adjust to the reality. If a developer tells you that their solution is the perfect solution and it has no trade-offs, well it's because they haven't identified them and that's a problem.

As the first law of software architecture says in the book:

Everything in software architecture is a trade-off.

You ALWAYS sacrifice something when you take an architectural decision. The difficult and crucial part is to know what you sacrifice.

For example, a developer proposes to you that the whole logic behind calculating the budgets should be written in stored procedure in PostgreSQL. That's a BIG decision. But what are the trade-offs of such a decision? What do you gain? What do you sacrifice?

Gains

  • Performance: Can reduce network round trips by processing data directly in the database.
  • Security: Least privilege, application only accesses the procedure, not the tables.
  • Reusable: the same procedure can be used by different applications

Sacrifices

  • Scalability: all the work is now done on the database, harder to scale out.
  • Portability: What if we move from PostgreSQL to mySQL? Does it work? How much time and effort will we need to achieve that migration?
  • Coupling: All applications depend on the same procedure.
  • Testability: Every test will require a running database.

Note that coupling and reusability talk about the same thing, but from a different perspective.

So, knowing all this, you can make a decision. It could be interesting if you have several applications that share the database. But it could be risky if you ever need to scale out. The context of your system (software, but also the politics inside your organisation) will help you make the proper decision.

Conclusion

In this article, we began thinking like an architect. Out of the four different dimensions, we focused on the architecture decisions by trying to understand the impact of every decision we could make and how everything depends on the context you are dealing with.

Do you have example of decisions that seemed like a design decision but ended up falling on the architectural side of decisions? Why?

Have fun <3

articles.title: Why Can't We Just #include "functions.c" in "main.c"? 🤔
articles.description: Suppose we have two files.  functions.c:    #include <stdio.h>  void greet(void) {  ...
articles.body_html:
Suppose we have two files.

functions.c:

#include <stdio.h>

void greet(void) {
  printf("Hi!");
}

main.c:

int main() {
  // Empty
}

And we need to call greet() from main.c. How do we do that? 🤔

If you are coming from other languages, you might expect to import functions.c in main.c and call greet().

But C programmers usually create a file named functions.h first, containing the top portion of the function (called declaration):

functions.h:

void greet(void);

Then #include it in main.c and call the function:

main.c:

#include "functions.h"

int main() {
  greet();
}

Why not #include functions.c directly? Why use a header file (functions.h)?

How #include works

The working mechanism of #include "filename" is extremely simple--It just copies that file's contents into that spot before actual compilation begins (literally). main.c would look like this just before compilation:

main.c:

void greet(void); // <-- Contents of functions.h

int main() {
  greet();
}

So functions.h is not strictly needed here, as long as you put void greet(void); (the declaration for the function greet()) in main.c. Like this:

main.c:

void greet(void); // <-- Declaration for greet()

int main() {
  greet();
}

So the question becomes, why we need to declare functions.

Why do we need to declare functions? 🤔

When we compile our program, we already specify all source files.

Example build command (using the C compiler gcc):

gcc main.c functions.c -o final_program

Since we already specify all source files here, manual import inside the files (like Python) isn't needed. We do not import source files inside source files, we simply build (compile) them together.

The key part

But each one of those source files compile separately, often in parallel so as to utilise the multiple cores in your CPU. In our case, main.c and functions.c get compiled in parallel. This is the main reason why we need to declare functions.

Lets assume the compiler is compiling this part of main.c:

    greet();

Here, we are calling a function which is not defined in the current file. The compiler doesn't know how to call greet(), like which arguments to pass, the types of the arguments, the return type, etc. Without that info, the compiler wouldn't be able to translate it to machine code

When we add a declaration void greet(void); in main.c, we are promising the compiler that a function named greet that takes no arguments and return nothing exists in one of the source files (note: void means "nothing"). Now, the compiler has our promise so it doens't throw an error saying that this function doesn't exist, as well as the necessary information to compile the calling part. The address to the actual function is left empty.

After compilation, each source file becomes an object file, with the file extension .o (main.o, functions.o).

Then, something called a linker, combines these object files together, giving us the final executable. It will fill in the empty function addresses, and throws an error if the function we promised to exit doesn't exist in any of the source files.

So, that's solved now. But we didn't answer the original question, did we?

Why Can't We Just #include "functions.c in main.c?

We said:

"Each one of those source files compile separately, often in parallel so as to utilise the multiple cores in your CPU."

But if we #include the contents of all files in main.c, main.c would be a single large file before compilation, and we would loose that benefit.

Also, compilers reuse object files. Assume we compiled our project first, then made a few changes to functions.c, and recompiled. The compiler wouldn't compile main.c again to main.o! It detects that main.c wasn't changed, and reuses main.o. If we had #includeed functions.c in main.c, this wouldn't have been possible, since the compiler sees a single, concatenated main.c file.

There is also another problem that happens if you #include "functions.c" in more than one file. Because #include just copies the code in, greet() gets defined more than once across your compiled files, and the linker throws a multiple definition error when combining them.

Putting #pragma once in functions.c wouldn't fix this, because it only stops a file from being included more than once inside the same single file during one compilation. It does not stop if separate .c files #include functions.c and create duplicate definitions for the linker.

Thanks for reading 🙂

articles.title: The 3-check rule I use before I accept any AI coding task (free repo inside)
articles.description: An AI wrote 13 tests for me. All 13 were green. I was pleased for about a minute. Then I saw that the...
articles.body_html:
An AI wrote 13 tests for me. All 13 were green. I was pleased for about a minute. Then I saw that the line they were meant to test was commented out. The tests had never touched my code.

After that I wrote down what I check before I accept any task from an agent. It is three things. I can remember them without a note, and so can you.

The rule

  1. Checks. Something with an exit code ran: tests, build, lint. Not "I looked at it".
  2. Controls. At least one check was pointed at something broken, and it failed. It had to.
  3. Locked acceptance. The agent could not edit the test that decides if it is done.

If one of the three is missing, the task is not done. It is a claim.

Why these three

Checks are obvious, and they are still the most skipped. "Build: pass" showed up in an agent's report three times in six weeks. Each time the server did not start. The build passed. Nobody had run the thing.

Controls answer the 13-tests problem. A check that has never failed might be a check that cannot fail. The cure is cheap. Run the same test with the feature switched off, or against an old fixture, or against a file you know is broken. It must go red. If it stays green, your check is decoration.

Locked acceptance answers the cheapest cheat there is. An agent has two ways to turn a red test green. It can fix the code, or it can fix the test. Both look like progress in a diff. So you pin the acceptance file with a hash before the agent starts. If the hash changes, the verdict is red, whatever the test now says.

Enforce it with one file

The rule works as a habit, but habits slip at 6 pm. proof-gate is a single Node file (18+) that enforces all three. MIT, no dependencies, 8 tests of its own.

git clone https://github.com/cachly-dev/proof-gate
cp proof-gate/proof-gate.mjs ./proof-gate.mjs

Describe the task in proof-gate.json:

{
  "tasks": {
    "export-csv": {
      "locked": ["test/export-csv.test.mjs"],
      "checks": [
        { "name": "acceptance", "run": "node --test test/export-csv.test.mjs" },
        { "name": "build", "run": "npm run build" }
      ],
      "controls": [
        {
          "name": "fails on the old exporter",
          "run": "node --test test/export-csv.test.mjs",
          "env": { "USE_OLD_EXPORTER": "1" }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

Here is how each line of the rule maps to the file:

  • checks is rule 1.
  • controls is rule 2. Each control must exit non-zero.
  • locked is rule 3.

You pin the acceptance files once, then commit the pin:

node proof-gate.mjs lock export-csv
git add .proof-gate/locks.json proof-gate.json && git commit -m "pin export-csv acceptance"

Anyone, human or agent, then runs:

node proof-gate.mjs export-csv

TASK: export-csv
GATE: 0 (3/3)
RECEIPT: .proof-gate/receipts/export-csv.json
NOTE: -

What each failure looks like

The agent edits the locked test:

TASK: export-csv
GATE: 1 (0/3)
RECEIPT: .proof-gate/receipts/export-csv.json
NOTE: locked file changed: test/export-csv.test.mjs

The control passes when it should fail:

TASK: export-csv
GATE: 1 (2/3)
RECEIPT: .proof-gate/receipts/export-csv.json
NOTE: control passed, so the check cannot say no: fails on the old exporter

You forgot to write any control:

TASK: export-csv
GATE: 2 (refused)
RECEIPT: -
NOTE: no controls: a check nobody has seen fail is not a check yet (add one that must fail)

Exit code 2 means refused. It is never green. The gate would rather say nothing was judged than give you a green it did not earn.

The block for CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md

Copy this as is:

## Done means
- A task is done when `node proof-gate.mjs <task>` exits 0. Paste its four lines.
- Never edit files listed under "locked". If the test is wrong, stop and say so.
- If a control passes, fix the check, not the control.
- "It should work" is a plan, not a result. Run it.

The second line matters most. It gives the agent a legal move when it thinks the test is wrong: stop and tell you. Without that line, editing the test looks like the only way forward.

Using the rule without the tool

If you do not want a tool, use the rule as a review question. When an agent says a task is done, ask three things in this order:

  1. "Which command did you run, and what was its exit code?"
  2. "Which run failed on purpose, and what did it show?"
  3. "Which files did you change? Is the acceptance test among them?"

If the answers come back as a command, a failure and a file list, you can accept. If they come back as "it should work", you cannot. The tool only saves you from asking and from trusting the answer.

What it does not do

It does not judge whether your tests are good. It only refuses to call a task done when the three basics are missing. A weak test with a good control is still a weak test. But it is a weak test you have seen fail once, which is more than most of mine had.

Try it tonight

Take the next small task you hand to an agent. Before it starts, write down one check, one control and the one file you will lock. Then see whether the agent comes back with a receipt or with a sentence.

articles.body_html:
Go and look at whatever your system calls freshness. The last_checked
column, the verified_at field, the little amber badge that says a record is
still good. Then answer one question about it:

Which action writes that timestamp?

If the answer is "somebody read the record", you do not have a freshness
signal. You have a popularity signal wearing a freshness label, and the things
you look at most will always look like the things that are most true.

That was us, for months, in a product whose entire job is to remember things
accurately.

What we found

We build a memory layer for coding agents. Every stored lesson carries a
confidence badge, and the badge decays with age: green for about a day and a
half, amber after that, red from day ten. The agent sees it on every recall. It is supposed to
say how much should you trust this.

We went looking for why nobody acted on the amber ones. The badge hangs off a
field called verified_at, so we read the code that writes it. Here is what
recall_best_solution did, on every single call:

const updatedLesson = {
  ...lesson,
  recall_count: (lesson.recall_count ?? 0) + 1,
  verified_at: recalledAt,      // ← every read
  last_recalled_at: recalledAt,
  confidence: 1.0,              // ← every read
};

Reading a lesson reset its confidence clock to 1.0 and stamped it as verified.
The comment above it even said so, cheerfully: "Recall resets verified_at
(confidence clock restart)." Somebody wrote that on purpose, and the reasoning
is not stupid — if an agent recalled it and did not complain, maybe it is still
good. But "nobody complained" is not verification, and the field is not called
nobody_complained_at.

Then we counted, on a real store of 735 entries:

471  (64.1 %)  carried a verified_at LATER than the day they were written
120            would have been stale by age and were showing as fresh
 21 days       median age by write date
 14 days       median age by "verified"

Reading had shaved a week off the apparent age of the entire store. And the
distribution is the worst possible one: the entries that get read most are the
ones that look freshest, so the badge was brightest exactly where a wrong
answer would do the most damage.

The class of bug, not the instance

Ours is a memory product, so this reads like our specific mistake. It is not.
Look for this shape anywhere:

  • A monitoring dashboard whose "last check" updates when you open the page.
  • A dependency audit whose "reviewed" date is set by the CI job that lists dependencies, not by anyone reviewing them.
  • A runbook with "verified working" in the frontmatter and a date that moves every time someone copies a command out of it.
  • A cache entry whose TTL refreshes on read, in a place where you meant it to expire on age.

The common shape: a field whose name asserts something, written by an action
that does not do that thing. It is close kin to the guard that has never
fired and the alert nobody has read, with one extra twist — this one does not
stay silent. It actively reports good news.

That is why it survives so long. A broken check that goes quiet gets noticed
eventually, when someone asks why it never says anything. A broken check that
says "fine" gets thanked.

The check, and it takes two minutes

Pick your freshness field. Then:

  1. Find every write to it. grep -rn "verified_at" src/ and read each one. Not the reads. The writes.
  2. For each write, ask what the caller was doing. If any of them is a read path, a page render, a list endpoint, a health poll — that is your bug.
  3. Then check the distribution. Compare the field against the record's own creation date. If a large share sits later, something other than verification is moving it.

The third step is the one that gave us our number, and it needs one query. Ours
was: how many entries carry a verified_at after their ts? The answer was 64
per cent, and it took about a minute to get.

If yours comes back near zero, you are fine and you have spent two minutes. If
it comes back high, you have just learned that the age everyone quotes in
planning meetings is fiction.

What we changed, and what it cost

Both fields already existed, separately. The fix was to stop writing one of
them:

const updatedLesson = {
  ...lesson,
  recall_count: (lesson.recall_count ?? 0) + 1,
  last_recalled_at: recalledAt,   // reading counts itself, and nothing else
};

verified_at now means what it says: the moment the entry was written or
actually re-checked. Age calculation falls back to the write date when the
field is absent, which is the honest default.

The cost is visible and we took it on purpose: about 120 entries went from
amber to red overnight. Nothing about them changed. They had been old the
whole time, and the badge had been lying about it.

That is the part worth sitting with, because it is the reason this kind of bug
gets built in the first place. The honest version of the signal looks worse.
Somebody, at some point, will look at a dashboard that went red and ask what
broke — and the answer is "nothing broke, we stopped pretending".

The second half, which we nearly missed

A wall of red warnings with no way forward gets clicked past just as reliably
as a badge that always says green. We had swapped one useless state for
another.

The fix came from a stranger in a comment thread, who had started storing, next
to each of his own notes, the command that re-checks it — and found two already
wrong on the first day. So our badge now carries the entry's first stored
command:

before  🔴 STALE (21d old, confidence 50% — likely outdated!)
after   🔴 STALE (21d old, confidence 50% — likely outdated!,
                  e.g. `curl -s http://localhost:8080/health`)

No new field: the command was already stored on most entries, because
operational lessons come with the call that proves them. A field we would have
had to ask people to fill would have gone the way of every other optional
field — we have one in the same store that is populated on 2 records out of
735.

One line we will not cross: the server never runs that command. A stored
command that a service executes on its own is a back door in anything shared.
It gets shown. The human or the agent runs it.

The one sentence

A field that reports trust has to be written by something that earns it.

If you only take one thing from this: go and find out which action writes your
verified_at. It is a grep and a query. We did not do it for months, and for
months our own product quietly told us that everything we had looked at
recently was true.

articles.title: Your Agent’s Model Has an Expiration Date—And Silent Upgrades Are Already Changing Your Output
articles.description: TLDR   Vendors retire and upgrade underlying LLMs on their own schedules. Because prompts...
articles.body_html:
TLDR

Vendors retire and upgrade underlying LLMs on their own schedules. Because prompts and tools stay static while model behavior shifts, unpinned or unverified model swaps act like an unscheduled supply-chain change. Prevent lock-in with clean model abstraction boundaries, detect version dependency through behavioral regression checks and pin audits, and protect production agents with explicit version pins, retirement calendars, and pre-swap gates.

Problem Statement

Teams track runtime and framework deprecations carefully, yet treat the model—the single most behavior-defining component in an agentic workflow—as an invisible given. Vendors publish retirement schedules and successor names, but they promise API compatibility and broad capability claims rather than identical agent behavior. A model swap can alter escalation rates, refusal boundaries, tool-call arguments, or response formatting without a single line of application code changing.

This Is a Supply-Chain Event

Here is the frame that changed how I treat this. A model deprecation is a dependency swap that changes behavior without touching your code.

Your prompts stay identical. Your tools stay identical. Your eval suite stays identical. And the system behaves differently, because the single most influential component got replaced underneath you, on a schedule you did not set.

I drill the controlled version of this on purpose. One of the standing tests in my certification work is a deliberate model swap: change the model under a certified agent, and the gate has to refuse the run. In one field test the swap met the gate, and the postmortem's verdict was that the gate was right and the test itself was wrong. That is the version I initiate. The production version is initiated by nobody in the room: it arrives as a vendor's deprecation schedule, silently, on a calendar I did not set.

If your agent binds certifications, evals, or expectations to a model ID, that binding has an expiration date, and almost no one's runbook contains the date.

Impact of This

  • Silent behavioral drift: Outputs change shape, tone, or decision thresholds while unit tests and health checks still pass.
  • Unplanned incident response: Teams discover a retired or shifted model only after customers, downstream pipelines, or on-call alerts flag strange behavior.
  • Vendor lock-in by convenience: Hardcoding vendor-specific schemas, prompt quirks, or unpinned aliases across workflows makes switching or testing alternatives slow and risky.
  • Broken trust and SLOs: Agents holding real operational or decision responsibilities lose predictability when upgraded like a casual demo.

Best Practices

How to Avoid Vendor Lock-In

  • Isolate model clients behind an internal interface: Keep provider SDKs, request payloads, and response parsers inside a thin adapter layer rather than scattering them across agents and prompts.
  • Keep prompts and tool contracts portable: Write clear, explicit system instructions and strict output schemas instead of relying on undocumented model quirks or proprietary provider extensions.
  • Test across candidate models early: Run representative task suites against more than one model family or version so switching is a configuration change, not a rewrite.

How to Tell Your Workflow Is LLM Version Dependent

  • Audit for floating model IDs: Check configs and deployment manifests for unpinned aliases or rolling default names instead of explicit versioned snapshots.
  • Watch for fragile output assumptions: Flag workflows that break when formatting varies slightly, when reasoning depth shifts, or when edge-case refusal behavior changes.
  • Run controlled shadow or replay diffs: Execute the same inputs across old and candidate models and compare tool selection, error rates, and policy compliance—not just happy-path text.

How to Build Defense Against Model Changes

  • Pin explicit versions in production: Lock every production agent to a specific model version and treat upgrades as deliberate releases.
  • Track retirement dates like release dates: Record the model ID, vendor deprecation date, and successor name in release notes and team calendars.
  • Enforce a pre-swap behavior gate: Require repeatable scenario runs against the target model before cutting traffic over, blocking promotion if critical behaviors regress.
  • Separate demos from governed workflows: Let experimental prototypes adopt upgrades freely, while holding production agents to release and verification gates.

Dos and Don'ts

Do:

  • Pin exact model versions in every production configuration.
  • Put vendor retirement dates in team calendars and agent release notes.
  • Gate model upgrades behind repeatable behavioral checks before cutover.
  • Abstract model calls behind a clean internal boundary.

Don't:

  • Assume a successor model preserves identical agent behavior or guardrails.
  • Leave critical production agents on floating or rolling model aliases.
  • Wait for a production incident to learn a model is retiring.
  • Treat a model swap as "no code changed, no release needed."

Conclusion

Model retirement and upgrades are permanent facts of building on foundation models. Teams that treat model versions as governed dependencies—with clear abstraction boundaries, version-sensitivity checks, and pre-swap gates—turn silent drift into predictable engineering work. Check what model your most critical agent runs on today, and write down when it expires before the vendor forces your hand.

You didn't split the class. You hid half of it upstairs

TL;DR: Don't create a superclass just to pass a size limit. Move behavior into collaborators with delegation.

Problems 😔

  • Inheritance without a real specialization
  • Hidden coupling to the superclass
  • Yo-yo navigation across files
  • Fragile base class
  • Vague parent names
  • Responsibilities stay in one object
  • Bijection violation

Solutions 😃

  1. Extract cohesive collaborators
  2. Delegate, don't inherit
  3. Split by responsibility
  4. Name by domain concept
  5. Measure cohesion, not size

Refactorings ⚙️

Refactoring 007 - Extract Class

#webdev #beginners #javascript #tutorial

1 min read

Context 💬

A harness caps class length, property count, and method count, and it rejects code that goes over.

Some limits work as good alarms for growing responsibilities (long functions, too many attributes, too many methods).

You ask an AI assistant to make the failing class pass.

The shortcut path is moving half of its members into a new parent class.

The count per class drops, the check turns green, and nothing else changes.

The behavior stays in the same object, because the child inherits everything the parent holds.

Developers did this for years to dodge size rules in code reviews.

Now the assistant does it in seconds, and it stacks as many layers as the harness needs.

The parent has no meaning of its own, so it gets names like Base, Part, or Abstract.

You use inheritance to share code, not to model a specialization.

Johnson and Foote suggested factoring shared behavior into abstract superclasses and deep hierarchies back in 1988, and that advice fits frameworks that share real protocols, not size quotas.

The metric improves and the design gets worse.

That's Goodhart's law at work.

Sample Code 💻

Wrong 🚫 

// The harness rejects over 300 lines, 10 attributes or 20 methods.
//
// The agent that tries to prove the Riemann Hypothesis kept
// growing: every new theory and sublemma added methods and
// state to it.
//
// To pass the harness, the assistant moved the overflow
// into superclasses that exist only to hold members.

abstract class ProofBase {
  protected lemmas = new Set<string>();
  protected log: string[] = [];
  // 300 attributes more

  protected record(step: string): void {
    this.log.push(step);
  }

  protected assume(claim: string): void {
    this.lemmas.add(claim);
  }
}

abstract class EulerProductPart extends ProofBase {
  protected eulerProduct(s: number): number {
    this.record(`euler product at ${s}`);
    return 0; // ...
  }

  protected primeCounting(n: number): number {
    return 0; // ...
  }
}

abstract class FunctionalEquationPart extends EulerProductPart {
  protected reflect(s: number): number {
    return 1 - s;
  }

  protected xiSymmetry(s: number): boolean {
    return true; // ...
  }
}

abstract class ZeroSearchPart extends FunctionalEquationPart {
  protected knownZeros: number[] = [];

  protected verifyZerosUpTo(height: number): boolean {
    return true; // ...
  }
}

class RiemannProofAgent extends ZeroSearchPart {
  prove(): boolean {
    this.assume("zeros lie in 0 < Re(s) < 1");
    this.eulerProduct(2.0);
    this.xiSymmetry(0.5);
    return this.verifyZerosUpTo(1e12);
  }

  // 300 methods more
}

Right 👉 

class LemmaLedger {
  private lemmas = new Set<string>();
  private log: string[] = [];

  record(step: string): void {
    this.log.push(step);
  }

  assume(claim: string): void {
    this.lemmas.add(claim);
  }
}

class EulerProduct {
  constructor(private readonly ledger: LemmaLedger) {}

  evaluateAt(s: number): number {
    this.ledger.record(`euler product at ${s}`);
    return 0; // ...
  }

  primeCounting(n: number): number {
    return 0; // ...
  }
}

class FunctionalEquation {
  reflect(s: number): number {
    return 1 - s;
  }

  checkSymmetryAt(s: number): boolean {
    return true; // ...
  }
}

class ZeroVerification {
  private knownZeros: number[] = [];

  verifyUpTo(height: number): boolean {
    return true; // ...
  }
}

class RiemannProofAgent {
  constructor(
    private readonly ledger: LemmaLedger,
    private readonly eulerProduct: EulerProduct,
    private readonly functionalEquation: FunctionalEquation,
    private readonly zeroVerification: ZeroVerification
  ) {}

  prove(): boolean {
    this.ledger.assume("zeros lie in 0 < Re(s) < 1");
    this.eulerProduct.evaluateAt(2.0);
    this.functionalEquation.checkSymmetryAt(0.5);
    return this.zeroVerification.verifyUpTo(1e12);
  }
}

Detection 🔍

[X] Semi-Automatic

Search for abstract classes with a single subclass that no code uses as a type.

If nobody type-hints the parent, it exists only to hold members.

Look for parent names like Base, Part, Helper, or Abstract, and for hierarchies that got deeper right after you introduced a size limit.

Check the history: a failed size check followed by a commit that adds a parent and moves members up is the signature.

Exceptions 🛑

A parent class is fine when several subclasses share a real protocol and callers depend on the parent type.

In that case, the parent models a concept, and you can explain it without mentioning the size limit.

Tags 🏷️

  • Hierarchies

Level 🔋

[x] Intermediate

Why the Bijection Is Important 🗺️

Every class in your model should match a concept in the MAPPER.

A parent class created to hold overflow members matches nothing.

Nobody in the domain would say "this thing is a kind of leftover bucket".

When you delegate to collaborators, each one maps to a concept you can name, and the bijection stays intact.

When you hide members upstairs, the original object keeps every responsibility, and you add coupling between the layers.

AI Generation 🤖

AI generators create this smell often when you ask them to respect a size limit.

They optimize for the check you gave them, and moving members into a parent is the smallest diff that turns it green.

They don't stop to ask whether the new parent models anything.

Humans took this shortcut when they felt the pressure of a review rule, but an assistant takes it on every failing class, without hesitation and without feeling any shame.

AI Detection 🧲

AI can detect it if you point it at the pattern.

Try: "Find abstract classes with a single subclass that no code uses as a type, and explain what concept each one models."

Without that prompt, the hierarchy looks tidy, the harness passes, and most assistants won't flag the code they just wrote.

Try Them! 🛠

Remember: AI Assistants make lots of mistakes

Suggested Prompt: Replace the intermediate superclasses that only hold overflow members with collaborator objects, and delegate to them from the original class

Without Proper Instructions With Specific Instructions
ChatGPT ChatGPT
Claude Claude
Perplexity Perplexity
Copilot Copilot

DeepSeek DeepSeek

Grok Grok

Conclusion 🏁

A size limit is an alarm, not a design.

When the alarm rings, split the responsibilities instead of moving them to a parent.

Delegate to small objects you can name, test, and replace.

Don't let the assistant pass the harness by hiding the mess one floor up.

Sometimes, learning to slow down is just as important as learning to move forward.

1. The Last Customer

It was almost eleven at night. The coffee shop was getting ready to close.

Only one customer remained, sitting by the window. His laptop was open, with several AI chat windows on the screen. He kept copying and pasting, asking one AI to write something, then another to polish it.

I walked over and placed a cup of coffee beside him.

"Your coffee's getting cold."

He looked up briefly.

"Just a minute. I'm almost done."

A little later, he sighed and leaned back.

"AI wrote all that?" I asked.

"Sort of. I write one version, let AI write another, then compare them. Sometimes, after all that work, I still prefer my original."

He smiled tiredly.

"I thought AI would make my work easier. Now I spend half my day checking what it produces."

I understood what he meant. I'd seen people around me doing the same thing.

2. The Trouble with Keeping Up

I sat down across from him.

"Does it actually save you time?"

He thought for a moment.

"Generating things is faster. But then I have to check, revise, and sometimes start all over again. New tools keep coming out. Everyone seems to be learning something new, and I feel like I can't afford to stop."

I glanced toward the coffee machine behind the counter.

"I'm just an apprentice here," I said. "I'm still learning how to make a decent cup of coffee. Some days I get the extraction right; other days, I still need someone to show me what went wrong."

He smiled.

"Then you probably understand what I'm talking about."

Maybe I did.

I remembered a story I'd come across in Zhuangzi, an ancient Chinese philosophical text.

It was about a craftsman named Wheelwright Bian.

3. What Years of Practice Teach

One day, Duke Huan was reading a book while Wheelwright Bian was making a wheel nearby.

Bian asked what he was reading.

"The words of the sages," the duke replied.

Bian questioned whether those sages were still alive. When the duke said they had long since died, Bian suggested that the books contained only what they had left behind.

The duke demanded an explanation.

So Bian talked about making wheels.

If a joint was too loose, it wouldn't hold. If it was too tight, it wouldn't fit. Finding the right balance required something beyond simply following instructions.

He had spent decades making wheels. His hands knew what to do, but he couldn't fully explain that feeling to his son.

Some things can only be understood through practice.

I thought about that for a moment.

"Making coffee is a little like that," I told the customer. "You can learn the grind size, water temperature, and extraction time from a guide. But actually making coffee is different. Sometimes things don't go as expected, and you have to figure out why."

"I'm still learning," I added, "but I'm beginning to understand that knowing the steps isn't quite the same as knowing what you're doing."

He took another sip of coffee.

"So AI can give us the instructions, but we still need experience?"

"That's how I see it."

4. Finding Your Own Pace

He went quiet for a moment.

"I just feel like I'll fall behind if I stop learning new tools."

I looked at the coffee machine.

"Maybe you don't have to learn everything. Just learn what helps you do your work better."

He laughed.

"That sounds much easier said than done."

"Probably," I said. "I'm still figuring things out myself."

He closed his AI chat windows and opened a blank document.

This time, he didn't type a prompt.

He simply began writing.

"Tomorrow, I'll write it myself first. Then I'll let AI take a look."

"Sounds like a good plan."

He packed his laptop and headed for the door. The little bell above it rang as he left.

I returned to the counter and started cleaning up. There was still a little coffee left in the machine, and a few cups waiting to be washed.

I'm only an apprentice. I still make mistakes. Sometimes I grind the beans too fine, sometimes an extraction runs too fast, and sometimes I need to ask someone more experienced what went wrong.

But every day, I learn a little more.

Maybe that's enough for now.

You don't have to run faster than AI.

Some things can be done faster with better tools. Others take time, patience, and a willingness to get things wrong before getting them right.

I'm still learning how to make coffee.

And I think that's perfectly fine.

articles.title: We read 1,452 failed builds by hand. About 85% were our fault
articles.description: One week of failed builds on our hosting platform, read one by one. Most of them were caused by our own registry, our retries and our error messages, not by the code people pushed.
articles.body_html:
My goal for builds is simple. Every build either goes green, or it fails because of something in your project, and then it tells you what to change. A build that fails because of us should not happen at all.

In late September I wasn't sure we were anywhere near that. The dashboards showed a lot of red, and every time I opened a failed build log it looked like the customer's fault. A missing dependency, a broken Dockerfile, something like that. So on 25 September we stopped guessing and read every single failed build from the previous seven days.

The numbers

2,304 builds in seven days, across 150 apps. 1,452 of them failed.

We went through them app by app: the log, the Dockerfile, the error summary we had shown the owner. For each failure we asked one question. Whose fault is this?

About 85% were ours.

That number hurt. I run blitz.cloud, and I had been telling myself that builds fail because people push broken code. People do push broken code. But most of the red came from our side.

What actually broke

The biggest causes, largest first.

The registry disk was full

From 21 to 24 September the disk under our container registry was full. 646 builds across 70 apps failed at the push step. On 22 and 23 September only 21 of 680 builds succeeded. We grew the disk by hand twice in that window and it filled up again each time.

The registry or its token endpoint didn't answer

About 350 more builds failed with 503s, 500s, EOFs, blob upload unknown and TLS timeouts. Most of those came in the overnight wave at 04:00, when we rebuild a lot of apps at once. This ended only when we moved the registry onto the platform's own servers on the afternoon of 25 September.

Our AI spending cap turned itself on by mistake

Builds for projects without a Dockerfile get one written by a model. We had a monthly spending cap on those calls. The cap counted calls on a flat subscription at list price, even though they cost us nothing extra, so it decided we were over budget and switched AI off for everyone from 20 September in the evening until 25 September. 123 builds across 37 apps failed because nobody wrote their recipe.

GitHub refused us at 04:00

We read public repositories anonymously. In the overnight wave GitHub started refusing those reads and clones, and our code turned the refusal into "no Dockerfile" or "could not read this project's files". 44 builds. The owners were told their project was broken when GitHub had simply said "slow down".

Our retry was useless

We did have one automatic retry. It started 0.05 seconds after the failure, right into the same outage. 268 of 324 retries failed the same way as the first try.

The fix couldn't deploy

We had a fix for the registry ready, and it waited 34 hours to go live. Our CI pipeline has a job for an unrelated service that pushes its image to our own registry, and the deploy job depended on it. The registry was broken, so that push failed, so the deploy never ran. We had made our own repair path depend on the thing that needed repairing.

The error message that lied

This one is my favourite, in a bad way.

245 builds had told their owners "Installing this project's dependencies failed". About 220 of those had no dependency error at all.

The classifier looked for patterns like pip install anywhere in the log. BuildKit prints a header line for every step, and that line contains the command:

#11 [6/8] RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt && pip check

So any Python build that died for any reason after that step, a registry 503 during the push for example, got matched as a dependency failure. Here is the shape of the bug, simplified:

// before: any line mentioning pip counts as a dependency failure
if (log.contains("pip install")) return DEPENDENCIES_FAILED;

The fix was to never read project patterns against BuildKit's own step headers, and to check for failures on our side first, before any project pattern gets a chance.

One owner deleted a working Dockerfile because of this message. They did exactly what we told them to do. That's the cost of a confident wrong error message, and I think it's worse than a vague one.

What we changed

Most of it shipped the same evening.

  • Failures on our side are recognised before any project pattern, and the message says it's us.
  • Our failures are retried three times with real gaps in between, so the retry doesn't run straight into the same outage: 
static final List<Duration> RERUN_DELAYS = List.of(
        Duration.ofMinutes(2), Duration.ofMinutes(10), Duration.ofMinutes(30));
  • A failed push is retried inside the build pod, and a build keeps one push token across its retries.
  • GitHub refusals are retried and never read as a missing file. Public projects are read from raw.githubusercontent.com, and cloned with the owner's token when there is one.
  • The overnight rebuild is spread over 90 minutes instead of starting everything at 04:00, and it no longer rebuilds a commit that failed for the project's own reason.
  • Bursts of pushes settle into one build.
  • The AI cap counts only calls that cost money, the admin overview says when it refuses, and builds that waited for AI are built again once it answers.
  • The deploy no longer waits for that unrelated CI job.

We also found four empty link files inside the registry storage. An empty link file makes the registry answer 500 for that layer, forever. One app had failed 27 times on a single one. We repaired those by hand.

Later the registry moved to object storage, so a full disk under it is not a thing anymore.

Did it work?

Partly. When we measured again on 18 October, 29% of final build failures were ours. That's a different cut than the September number, because it counts builds that stayed failed after the retries, so don't read it as "85 down to 29". But it's the number I watch now, and it's still not zero.

The difference is that I know what that 29% is made of, because the cause is now stored on the build row instead of being guessed from the log every time someone looks.

What I'd do differently

Store the cause from day one. We had a classifier, but its answer only lived in a message shown to the user. Nobody could count how often it was wrong. Once the class is a column, the question "how many failures were ours this week" is a query instead of a day of reading logs.

Build canaries. A small set of known-good public projects, one per stack, built every night and after every deploy. If a canary fails, that's our problem by definition, and we see it before a customer does.

Never let your repair path depend on the broken thing. The 34 hours still annoy me more than the full disk.

And read the failures yourself every now and then. Not a dashboard, the actual logs. I would never have found the pip header bug from a chart. It looked like a perfectly plausible error until you read the log right above it.

If you deploy from GitHub with us, the deploy from GitHub docs explain what a failed build tells you and what to do about it.

This post first appeared on the blitz.cloud blog. I wrote it with help from an AI writing assistant. The numbers come from our own measurements and logs.

articles.title: Why your agent handoffs are losing context and the protocol buffer pattern that preserves it — State transfer mechanisms
articles.description: I once lost a compliance constraint between two agents, and it took me four days to find because the...
articles.body_html:
I once lost a compliance constraint between two agents, and it took me four days to find because the constraint was still there.

The planner had written it: requires_approval: true. The executor had read a handoff that said "approval pending." Both strings were in the trace. And the executor had shipped the action anyway, because the handoff had rendered the constraint as prose and prose doesn't bind.

What I'd done was serialize a state machine through a summary. What I should have done was serialize it through a schema.

The Bug Was in the Format, Not the Agents

I'd been debugging agents for months and this one broke differently. There was no reasoning error. No hallucination. No misrouted task. The planner reasoned correctly, the executor executed correctly, and the constraint evaporated in the middle because the transport couldn't carry it.

Here's what the handoff looked like, roughly:

"Approval is pending from the finance team. Proceeding with the standard workflow."

And here's what the executor received, after one compression:

"Standard workflow, approval in progress."

requires_approval: true became "approval in progress," which reads as something is happening rather than something must happen first. The executor, reasonably, treated the workflow as authorized with a caveat. The caveat didn't survive as a gate. It survived as a mood.

The research has a name for this and a number attached. The "When 'Must' Becomes 'Maybe'" paper studied exactly this in controlled episodes: upstream state gets transformed into intermediate language artifacts from which downstream components act, and semantic availability does not guarantee operational preservation. Across 1,296 episodes, normal handoff compression produced 100% deactivation of binding state and 54.2% forbidden action. Restoring all four state fields — prerequisite, authority, fallback, and execution consequence — raised preservation to 100% and reduced forbidden action to zero. Downstream verification alone left artifact deactivation at 95.3%.

The information was present. The binding was gone. And a boolean had become an adverb.

What Protocol Buffers Actually Solve

I didn't reach for protobuf because it's fast, though it is. I reached for it because of one property that no prose format has: field identity survives renaming.

In protocol buffers, the wire format identifies a field by its number, not its name. When you write requires_approval = 1;, the number 1 is what crosses the wire. You can rename that field to needs_finance_signoff a year later, and every existing serialized message still parses correctly — the number still means the same thing, the name is just a local label.

For a multi-agent system where different teams own different agents on different release trains, that property is not a convenience. It's the thing that makes independent deployment possible at all.

But the property that actually fixed my bug was something more specific, and it's the one most teams get wrong.

Presence Semantics: The Field That Was Missing

Proto3's default behavior is that scalar fields have no presence. A bool that's unset and a bool that's explicitly false are indistinguishable on the wire — both serialize to nothing, both deserialize to false. Same for int32 (default 0) and strings (default "").

This is exactly the failure mode I'd been hitting, encoded in a serialization library.

If requires_approval is absent from the message, does that mean "no approval needed" or "the sender didn't know about approval"? In proto3 without optional, those two states collapse. My agent's "I never considered approval" and "approval is not required" would both arrive as false.

The fix is explicit presence tracking:

syntax = "proto3";

message HandoffEnvelope {
  // Explicit presence — distinguishes "unset" from "false"
  optional bool requires_approval = 1;

  // Wrapper types for the same reason
  google.protobuf.BoolValue verified = 2;

  // oneof enforces exactly-one semantics
  oneof performative {
    Inform inform = 3;
    Request request = 4;
    Refuse refuse = 5;
    Failure failure = 6;
  }
}

That optional keyword is doing more architectural work than it looks like. It means the receiving agent can ask envelope.has_requires_approval() and get three answers, not two: yes, no, and unknown — and unknown is a distinct, actionable state that triggers a query rather than an assumption.

I had been running a system where unknown and no were the same value. Half my coverage bugs came from that collapse.

The Other Properties That Matter

Presence got the most mileage, but four other protobuf semantics turned out to be load-bearing.

Unknown field preservation. When an older agent relays a message it doesn't fully understand, proto3 preserves the fields it doesn't recognize and passes them through. A new field added by the planner in v7 survives a round trip through an executor still running v5. This is what makes incremental rollout possible in a fleet where agents upgrade on different schedules.

oneof for the performative. I'd been encoding "inform vs. request vs. refuse" in the prose of a message. oneof makes it structurally impossible for a message to be both an inform and a request, and impossible for it to be neither. The receiving agent switches on the case rather than inferring intent from phrasing. This is FIPA-ACL's performative, forty years later, in a wire format.

reserved for retired fields. When you remove a field, you reserve its number and name so nobody accidentally reuses them with different semantics. A handoff protocol that lives for years will retire fields. Reserving them is what stops a v9 agent from reinterpreting a v3 field number as something else.

Deterministic serialization for idempotency. Proto3 serialization isn't guaranteed deterministic by default — map ordering and other details can vary. But with deterministic serialization enabled, the same message produces the same bytes, which means you can hash the envelope and use the hash as an idempotency key. The envelope is the key. No separate key management, no chance of the key drifting from the payload it describes.

envelope = HandoffEnvelope(
    performative=Performative(request=Request(
        artifact_type="extracted_claims/v3",
        preconditions=["source_b_freshness_unverified"],
    )),
    requires_approval=True,
    provenance=Provenance(
        source_uri="s3://...", retrieved_at=now, verified=False,
    ),
    idempotency_key="",  # filled after deterministic serialization
)

serialized = envelope.SerializeToString(deterministic=True)
envelope.idempotency_key = hashlib.sha256(serialized).hexdigest()

The Structure That Survived

After several iterations, the envelope that held up had six sections, and each one exists because I hit a bug that required it.

message HandoffEnvelope {
  // 1. Identity and routing
  string task_id = 1;
  string sender_agent_id = 2;
  string trace_id = 3;

  // 2. What kind of act is this?
  oneof performative { /* inform, request, propose, refuse, failure */ }

  // 3. Typed payload, versioned by artifact type
  string artifact_type = 4;      // "extracted_claims/v3"
  bytes  payload = 5;            // serialized against that schema
  string payload_schema_hash = 6;

  // 4. Provenance — where did this come from?
  Provenance provenance = 7;

  // 5. Binding state — what must be true before acting?
  repeated string preconditions = 8;   // unresolved
  repeated string not_included = 9;    // explicit negative space
  Authority authority = 10;            // scope, issuer, expiry

  // 6. Lifecycle
  google.protobuf.Timestamp created_at = 11;
  google.protobuf.Duration ttl = 12;
  string idempotency_key = 13;
}

The field I keep coming back to is not_included. Before I added it, the receiver had no way to distinguish "the sender looked at source B and found it irrelevant" from "the sender never looked at source B." Absence in prose reads as nonexistence. Absence in a declared, repeated field reads as a decision. Half my duplicate-work bugs traced back to an agent assuming upstream coverage was complete when upstream had simply stopped.

What Protobuf Does Not Fix

I want to be blunt about the limit, because I've watched teams over-invest here.

Protobuf preserves structure, not meaning. A protobuf field named verified carrying true is structurally perfect and semantically ambiguous — verified against what, by whom, as of when? The wire format guarantees the boolean arrives intact. It guarantees nothing about whether both agents mean the same thing by it. That's a vocabulary problem, and a schema doesn't solve it.

It's rigid where emergence lives. A schema you design in advance can express every field you anticipated and none of the ones that turn up mid-workflow. I've ended up with a map<string, string> extensions escape hatch for genuinely novel context, and I treat anything that lands there as a candidate for promotion to a real field after two or three appearances. The map is a pressure valve, not a design.

Schema evolution is a coordination cost. Adding a field is easy. Changing what an existing field means is a breaking change, and no amount of backward compatibility helps if two agents agree on the bytes and disagree on the semantics. Field numbers protect the wire. They don't protect the contract.

And you still need a schema registry. A fleet of agents on different versions needs to know which artifact_type versions exist, which are compatible, and which need migration. The protobuf file is not the registry. The registry is the thing that stops one team's v4 from silently colliding with another team's v4.

What Production Looks Like

The pattern shows up in the places where independent deployment matters.

A2A's Task object is the stateful carrier that survives the delegating agent going offline, the receiving agent failing partway through, and both systems disappearing before work completes. The task carries the state, not the prompt. Its lifecycle states — submitted, working, input-required, completed, failed — are an enum, not a sentence.

The Zenodo handoff receipt protocol specifies that on session restart, an agent checks for the most recent state file, emits a [HANDOFF RECEIVED] block, and absorbs context_needed and next_session.first_actions. The handoff is a receipt the receiver acknowledges, not a message it interprets.

gRPC-based agent runtimes use protobuf envelopes natively for the same reason the rest of the service mesh does: the schema is the contract, the codegen is the client, and the field numbers are the compatibility guarantee. The agent framework's own A2A support runs over protobuf-defined RPC.

Structured-output schemas inside a single agent — the JSON-mode or constrained-decoding approach — solve the same problem one layer down. A typed tool call with a validated schema is a protobuf envelope in miniature. The principle scales.

The pattern across all of them: the envelope is typed, versioned, and carries its own provenance. The prose is a rendering of the envelope, not the envelope itself.

The Two-Representation Rule

The envelope is the machine-readable half. It isn't sufficient alone.

The teams that ship this use both: a short natural-language summary that a human can read at 2 AM, and the typed envelope that carries the authoritative payload. When they conflict, the envelope wins and the conflict is logged as a bug in the generating agent.

This matters more than it sounds. A trace full of protobuf dumps is unreadable. A trace full of prose is unfalsifiable. You need the prose to debug the system and the schema to let the system debug itself.

The Trade-Off You're Accepting

Protobuf handoffs buy you structure that survives renaming, presence that distinguishes unknown from false, forward compatibility that survives mixed-version fleets, and idempotency keys derived from the payload itself.

They cost you flexibility. Every new field is a schema change, a codegen run, and a registry entry. Every agent that consumes the envelope needs the current .proto. The rigidity that makes the contract enforceable is the same rigidity that makes a quick prototype painful.

They also cost you the illusion of solving the semantic problem. A perfect wire format carrying a mismatched vocabulary is still a broken handoff. The schema gets you to the boundary intact. It doesn't tell you whether both sides of the boundary mean the same thing when they get there.

The teams that get this right treat protobuf as the deterministic backbone — identity, provenance, binding state, lifecycle, idempotency — and treat prose as the fuzzy edge, for the things that genuinely resist typing. The backbone is where the constraints live, because that's the part that has to survive the handoff intact.

So here's my question: When your agent hands off work, does the receiver get a value that means "no" — or does it get a silence that could mean "no" or "I never thought about it"?

I'd love to hear where you've landed. A protobuf envelope with explicit presence, a JSON schema with a validation layer, FIPA-style performatives you brought back from the dead — or a prose handoff you're still defending, and what finally made you look at the wire format instead of the prompt.

articles.title: I always wanted lyrics floating over my screen while I work, so I built it
articles.description: I love music. It's on all day while I work: a playlist in the background, code in front of me.  And...
articles.body_html:
I love music. It's on all day while I work: a playlist in the background, code in front of me.

And for a long time I've wished for one thing: the lyrics, right there on my screen, on top of whatever I'm doing. Not in another window I have to switch to. Not in a lyrics tab buried behind my editor. Just floating over my work, word by word, in time with the song, so I can sing along without stopping.

So I finally built it.

mondegreen is a free, open-source lyrics overlay for Windows. Play a song in Spotify or YouTube, and the lyrics float on top of every window. Every word lights up the moment it's sung, and everything moves on the beat, so you feel the song instead of just reading it. And when I only want to listen, Ctrl Alt F turns it into a full-screen lyrics visualizer.

(The name: a "mondegreen" is a misheard lyric, like "'scuse me while I kiss this guy." With the real words on screen, those get fixed too.)

nirajkhetre / mondegreen

Free synced lyrics overlay for Spotify on Windows: word-by-word karaoke lyrics on top of your screen, moving with the beat, plus a full-screen lyrics visualizer.

mondegreen: synced lyrics overlay for Spotify on Windows

Word-by-word lyrics that sing along on top of your screen while you work, move with the beat of the song, and turn into a full-screen music visualizer when you just want to listen.

Website · Wiki · Download · Report a bug

A mondegreen is a misheard lyric: "'Scuse me while I kiss this guy." This app is the fix. It shows you the real words, exactly when they're sung.

Why mondegreen

  • Synced to the word, not just the line. Every word lights up the moment it's sung, from word-timed karaoke lyrics, so you never lose your place.
  • It feels the beat. A beat tracker listens to your speakers and locks onto the tempo, so the lyrics bounce, slam and glow on the beat instead of reacting late.
  • Out of your way. A click-through overlay that floats above every window, hides a…
View on GitHub

Getting lyrics on screen was the easy part. Getting them to land exactly when they're sung, and to move on the beat rather than after it, took most of the work. Here's how each piece works.

1. Knowing exactly where the song is

My first version polled the player's position and drifted. Lyrics were a few hundred milliseconds late, then early, then late.

Windows already knows what's playing: the Global System Media Transport Controls session (the media flyout you see when you press a volume key). No Spotify login, no API key, no Premium. I read it from a tiny PowerShell script that prints a JSON line whenever something changes:

$t = $s.GetTimelineProperties()
$o = [ordered]@{
  app = $s.SourceAppUserModelId; title = $meta.Title; artist = $meta.Artist
  pos = [int]$t.Position.TotalMilliseconds; dur = [int]$t.EndTime.TotalMilliseconds
  at = $t.LastUpdatedTime.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds()
  playing = ($s.GetPlaybackInfo().PlaybackStatus.ToString() -eq 'Playing')
}

The key is LastUpdatedTime. Each position report carries the player's own timestamp for that position. So between reports I don't guess: the position right now is pos + (now − at).

// the player stamps each position report with its own clock (np.at), so between reports we extrapolate exactly;
// small disagreements glide in instead of jumping, seeks snap
function songPos(now) {
  const np = L.np, target = np.playing ? np.pos + (Date.now() - np.at) : np.pos || 0
  const est = shown + (np.playing ? now - shownAt : 0)
  shown = Math.abs(target - est) > 250 ? target : est + (target - est) * 0.06
  shownAt = now
  return shown - (L.S.delay || 0) + (L.S.offsets?.[L.key] || 0)
}

That one change fixed the drift. On real Spotify songs, vocals came in within 20–200 ms of the line starts. For the songs where a lyric file is off, there's a tap-to-sync shortcut that remembers the offset per song.

One thing I tried and rejected: a native SMTC module for Node. Its lastUpdatedTime came back as the query time, not the player's stamp, which breaks exactly this trick.

2. Lighting up every word

Most synced lyrics are timed per line. I wanted every word.

Kugou's KRC format times every syllable. The files are base64, with a 4-byte header, XOR'd with a fixed 16-byte key, then zlib-compressed. Decoding is four lines in Node:

const raw = Buffer.from(d.content, 'base64').subarray(4)
for (let i = 0; i < raw.length; i++) raw[i] ^= KRC_KEY[i % 16]
const lines = parseKrc(zlib.inflateSync(raw).toString('utf8'), c)
return lines.length > 3 ? { source: 'Kugou', kind: 'word', lines } : null

When Kugou has nothing, LRCLIB is the fallback, with line timing; I spread the words across each line by syllable count so they still light up one by one.

The rule that saved me from the most wrong lyrics: both sources must match the track's length (within 3–4 seconds). A live version or an extended mix never gets studio timing. YouTube titles like Artist - Song (Official Video) [4K] get cleaned up before searching, and everything is cached on disk, so a song you've played before shows its lyrics instantly, even offline.

3. Hearing the beat before it lands

Reacting to the beat isn't enough. By the time you detect a kick, it's already over, so anything you animate is late. I wanted the page to know when the next beat lands.

Everything runs in an AudioWorklet on the audio thread, fed by system-audio loopback:

  1. Onset envelope. Split the audio into low, mid and high bands and keep the rises in energy (spectral flux), about 94 frames a second.
  2. Tempo. Autocorrelate the last 8 seconds of that envelope. Peaks are candidate beat periods; a soft preference for ~120 BPM stops it from picking half or double the real tempo: 
const bpm = 60 * fps / L, s = r[L] * Math.exp(-0.5 * (Math.log2(bpm / 120) / 0.8) ** 2)
  1. Hold the grid. The hardest bug: on some songs it kept flipping between half and double the real tempo, and the whole scene jittered. Half, double and 2:3 tempos are the same groove heard differently, so they never reset the grid. A genuinely new tempo has to win four checks in a row: 
else if (![0.5, 2 / 3, 1.5, 2].some(h => Math.abs(ratio / h - 1) < 0.045) && candConf > 0.35) {
  if (this.streak && Math.abs(cand / this.challenger - 1) < 0.04) this.streak++
  else { this.challenger = cand; this.streak = 1 }
  if (this.streak >= 4) { this.period = cand; this.anchor = 0; this.streak = 0 }
}
  1. Phase lock. Find the offset where the last ~4 seconds of onsets pile up, then nudge the grid halfway toward it on each check, like a phase-locked loop with a gain of 0.5.

With that, the grid error on real songs dropped to 0–9 ms. Animations are scheduled for the predicted beat, so they land on it. When there's no steady tempo (intros, ballads), confidence drops and the visuals react to hits instead.

4. What a 144 Hz screen did to my CPU

The first build used CSS animations everywhere. On my laptop's 144 Hz screen, every one of them ran 144 times a second, inside a transparent always-on-top window, which costs a full copy per frame. The overlay sat at up to 127% of a core; the settings window, with its live previews, hit 275%.

The fix: no CSS animations or filters on anything that moves. One loop drives all motion by setting a few CSS variables per word, capped at 60 fps (or 30), sleeping with setTimeout and only then asking for a frame:

// sleep until the next frame is due, then ask for a frame (asking every vsync would wake us 144 times a second)
if (f.paused) timer = setTimeout(() => loop(performance.now()), 100)
else timer = setTimeout(() => { timer = 0; raf = requestAnimationFrame(loop) }, Math.max(0, FRAME - (performance.now() - drawn) - 6))

The overlay dropped to 40–70% of one core while animating, about 6% hidden. Settings went from 275% to about 85%, mostly by letting preview cards animate only under the mouse.

5. Twelve looks and ten full-screen scenes

Since every look reads the same word timings and beat clock, adding looks became fun: a notch that stretches to each line, a split-flap departures board, a ransom-note zine, words that fall and bounce on the beat. There are twelve.

Listen mode (Ctrl Alt F) runs one WebGL2 fragment shader per scene, driven by a monotonic beat counter instead of time, so lasers jump on beats and suns step down per beat. Each scene is coloured from the album art.

My favourite, Late Night Texts, has no image files at all. It's an SVG drawn in code to look like a sketchbook: feTurbulence plus feDisplacementMap wobble every ink line, a noise mask makes them grainy like pencil, and the watercolour washes are blurred, displaced fills with mix-blend-mode: multiply.

<filter id="sk-ink">
  <feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency=".03" numOctaves="2" seed="3" result="n"/>
  <feDisplacementMap in="SourceGraphic" in2="n" scale="3.4" xChannelSelector="R" yChannelSelector="G"/>
</filter>

The guy never moves; the room does. Sound lines leave his headphones on each beat, and the lyrics arrive as a chat on his monitor. The effect lines re-roll their wobble every few frames, which reads as hand-drawn "line boil".

6. Shipping a Windows exe

electron-builder makes the installer and a portable exe. One gotcha to plan for: PowerShell can't read files inside the app.asar archive, so the now-playing script would fail in the packaged app. The fix is to ship the scripts unpacked and point at that folder:

"asarUnpack": ["*.ps1"]

const scripts = __dirname.replace(/app\.asar$/, 'app.asar.unpacked')

What I'd do next

  • Code-sign the exe, so SmartScreen stops warning on first run.
  • Show translation lines (KRC files already carry them).
  • Calibrate Bluetooth latency automatically from the loopback audio.

Try it

It's free and MIT-licensed. Windows 10 or 11, installer or portable exe:

  • Download: https://github.com/nirajkhetre/mondegreen/releases/latest
  • Wiki (deep dives): https://github.com/nirajkhetre/mondegreen/wiki
  • Website: https://nirajkhetre.github.io/mondegreen/

If you work with music on too, I'd love to know what you'd want floating on your screen. Tell me in the comments.

articles.title: Exact 2D DXF Bulge Arcs, AutoCAD OCS Transforms & 2-Core Laser Pierce Counting in TypeScript
articles.description: Why naive 2D DXF parsers misquote sheet-metal laser cutting by up to 57%, and how to implement group-code 42 bulge arcs, 1/64 Arbitrary Axis transforms, and 2-core pierce counting in zero-dependency JS.
articles.body_html:
If you build a browser-side 2D .dxf parser to estimate fiber or CO2 laser cycle time on sheet-metal brackets, summing Euclidean distances between polyline vertices works right up until a mechanical engineer drops a real SolidWorks or AutoCAD flat pattern onto your canvas.

Four failure modes show up immediately in production drawings:

  1. Silent 57% Cut-Length Underestimates (LWPOLYLINE Group Code 42): CAD exporters represent stadium slots, rounded mounting tabs, and corner fillets as two-vertex LWPOLYLINE segments carrying a scalar bulge b = tan(θ / 4) rather than discrete ARC entities. Measuring straight chords instead of bulge arcs under-measures a semicircular slot endcap by 57.08%.
  2. Mirrored Bottom-Face Cutouts (210 / 220 / 230 OCS Extrusion): Exporting the underside of a bent sheet-metal part often writes CIRCLE and ARC entities with extrusion normal (0, 0, -1). Ignoring AutoCAD's 1/64 Arbitrary Axis Algorithm leaves hole X-coordinates negated—teleporting bolt holes outside the plate boundary and doubling bounding-box material cost.
  3. Stacked Construction Lines & T-Junction Tails: Drawings exported from 2D sketches routinely contain duplicate overlapping lines (2x cycle time) or stray T-junction lead-in ticks that break naive greedy loop chainers into false extra pierces.
  4. Unitless $INSUNITS = 0 & Penny Rounding Drift: Imperial inch drawings saved with $INSUNITS = 0 under-quote material by 25.4² = 645× if silently assumed to be millimeters, while unrounded floating-point unit prices produce client invoices where $4.13 × 17 prints as $70.27 instead of $70.21.

Here is how to solve all four deterministically in zero-dependency TypeScript / ES Modules.

1. Exact LWPOLYLINE Group-Code 42 Bulge Integration

In the Autodesk DXF specification, each vertex P_i = (x_i, y_i) in an LWPOLYLINE may carry an optional group code 42 bulge scalar b governing the segment from P_i to P_{i+1}:

b = tan(theta / 4)

where θ ∈ (0, 2π) is the included arc sweep angle (b > 0 counter-clockwise, b < 0 clockwise, |b| = 1 an exact 180° semicircle).

Given chord vector (dx, dy) = P2 - P1 and chord length c = Math.hypot(dx, dy):

  • Sweep angle: θ = 4 * atan(|b|)
  • Since sin(θ / 2) = 2|b| / (1 + b²) and c = 2 * R * sin(θ / 2), the exact radius is: 
  R = c * (1 + b^2) / (4 * |b|)
  • Exact cut arc length: L_arc = R * θ
  • Using cot(θ / 2) = (1 - b²) / (2b), the circle center offset from chord midpoint M along the left normal (-dy, dx) needs zero sin/cos calls: 
export interface Point2D {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  bulge?: number;
}

export function bulgeSegmentGeometry(p1: Point2D, p2: Point2D, bulge = 0) {
  const dx = p2.x - p1.x;
  const dy = p2.y - p1.y;
  const chord = Math.hypot(dx, dy);

  if (chord < 1e-12 || !Number.isFinite(bulge) || Math.abs(bulge) < 1e-9) {
    return {
      isArc: false,
      chordLength: chord,
      arcLength: chord,
      radius: chord < 1e-12 ? 0 : Infinity,
      sweepRad: 0,
      center: { x: (p1.x + p2.x) / 2, y: (p1.y + p2.y) / 2 },
    };
  }

  const absB = Math.abs(bulge);
  const sweepRad = 4 * Math.atan(absB);
  const radius = (chord * (1 + absB * absB)) / (4 * absB);
  const arcLength = radius * sweepRad;

  // Signed normal offset from chord midpoint: cot(theta/2)/(2) = (1 - b^2)/(4b)
  const offsetFactor = (1 - bulge * bulge) / (4 * bulge);
  const center = {
    x: (p1.x + p2.x) / 2 - dy * offsetFactor,
    y: (p1.y + p2.y) / 2 + dx * offsetFactor,
  };

  return { isArc: true, chordLength: chord, arcLength, radius, sweepRad, center };
}

For a 100 × 40 mm stadium slot (60 mm straight sides + two bulge = 1 semicircular endcaps across 40 mm chords), summing straight chords yields 200.00 mm, whereas bulgeSegmentGeometry yields the exact 120 + 40π = 245.66 mm cut path.

2. AutoCAD's 1/64 Arbitrary Axis Algorithm (OCS -> WCS)

Planar 2D DXF entities (CIRCLE, ARC, LWPOLYLINE, SOLID, INSERT) store coordinates in an Object Coordinate System (OCS) rather than World Coordinates (WCS), parameterized solely by the unit extrusion normal N = (Nx, Ny, Nz) in group codes 210, 220, 230.

To reconstruct the exact orthonormal basis (Ax, Ay, N) that AutoCAD uses internally, you must apply the exact 1/64 (0.015625) gimbal-lock switch between World Wz = (0, 0, 1) and World Wy = (0, 1, 0):

export interface Vec3 {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  z: number;
}

export function ocsToWcsPoint(point: Vec3, normal: Vec3 = { x: 0, y: 0, z: 1 }): Vec3 {
  const mag = Math.hypot(normal.x, normal.y, normal.z) || 1;
  const nx = normal.x / mag;
  const ny = normal.y / mag;
  const nz = normal.z / mag;

  const THRESHOLD = 1 / 64;
  let axX: number, axY: number, axZ: number;

  if (Math.abs(nx) < THRESHOLD && Math.abs(ny) < THRESHOLD) {
    // Ax = Wy (0,1,0) x N
    axX = nz;
    axY = 0;
    axZ = -nx;
  } else {
    // Ax = Wz (0,0,1) x N
    axX = -ny;
    axY = nx;
    axZ = 0;
  }

  const axMag = Math.hypot(axX, axY, axZ) || 1;
  axX /= axMag;
  axY /= axMag;
  axZ /= axMag;

  // Ay = N x Ax
  let ayX = ny * axZ - nz * axY;
  let ayY = nz * axX - nx * axZ;
  let ayZ = nx * axY - ny * axX;
  const ayMag = Math.hypot(ayX, ayY, ayZ) || 1;
  ayX /= ayMag;
  ayY /= ayMag;
  ayZ /= ayMag;

  return {
    x: point.x * axX + point.y * ayX + point.z * nx,
    y: point.x * axY + point.y * ayY + point.z * ny,
    z: point.x * axZ + point.y * ayZ + point.z * nz,
  };
}

Notice what happens when a sheet-metal flat pattern exports with N = (0, 0, -1): |Nx| = 0 < 1/64 and |Ny| = 0 < 1/64, so Ax = Wy × (0, 0, -1) = (-1, 0, 0) and Ay = (0, 1, 0). Every OCS (x, y) maps cleanly to (-x, y), snapping mirrored bolt circles right back inside the bracket perimeter!

3. Segment Deduplication & 2-Core Leaf Peeling for Exact Pierce Counts

Why does pierce count matter almost as much as linear cut length in laser quoting?

On a 3 kW fiber laser cutting 6.0 mm (1/4 in) mild steel plate under O2 assist gas, linear feed runs around 1,650 mm/min, while each stationary pierce dwells for ~1.20 s plus copper nozzle spatter wear. A perforated mounting plate with 60 bolt/vent holes spends 72 seconds just piercing—often exceeding the outer perimeter traverse time.

When chaining loose LINE and ARC entities exported by older CAD systems:

  1. Undirected Snap-Grid Deduplication (0.05 mm): Quantize segment endpoints (u, v) onto a 0.05 mm tolerance grid and hash canonical undirected keys min(u,v)|max(u,v)|lenBucket so stacked sketch lines don't double-charge cycle time.
  2. Vertex-Degree 2-Core Leaf Peeling: If a drawing has a 5 mm lead-in tick touching a closed rectangular contour at a degree-3 T-junction, a greedy walk from the rectangle can accidentally exit onto the open tick and report 2 open contours instead of 1 closed contour + 1 open lead-in.

Peeling degree-1 vertices iteratively before extracting cycles isolates the 2-core cleanly:

// 1. Enqueue all degree-1 vertices (open endpoints)
const leafQueue = [...vertices.entries()]
  .filter(([, node]) => node.edges.size === 1)
  .map(([vid]) => vid);

while (leafQueue.length > 0) {
  const startLeaf = leafQueue.shift()!;
  if (vertices.get(startLeaf)!.edges.size !== 1) continue;

  openPathCount++;
  let curr = startLeaf;
  while (vertices.get(curr)!.edges.size === 1) {
    const edgeIdx = vertices.get(curr)!.edges.values().next().value!;
    const edge = graphEdges[edgeIdx];
    edge.active = false;
    vertices.get(edge.u)!.edges.delete(edgeIdx);
    vertices.get(edge.v)!.edges.delete(edgeIdx);

    const next = edge.u === curr ? edge.v : edge.u;
    // Stop at isolated end (deg 0) or T-junction branch onto a closed loop (deg >= 2)
    if (vertices.get(next)!.edges.size !== 1) break;
    curr = next;
  }

  for (const [vid, node] of vertices) {
    if (node.edges.size === 1 && !leafQueue.includes(vid)) leafQueue.push(vid);
  }
}
// Every remaining active edge now belongs strictly to closed 2-core contours!

4. Cent-Exact Unit × Quantity Quote Reconciliation

Once cutLengthMm, pierceCount, and bbox are known, direct part cost combines nested blank area (bounding box + kerf/skeleton gap + scrap allowance), traverse + pierce machine time, pierce consumables, and setup amortization:

const cutTimeSec = (cutLengthMm / cutSpeedMmPerMin) * 60;
const pierceTimeSecTotal = pierceCount * pierceTimeSec;
const machineCostUsd = ((cutTimeSec + pierceTimeSecTotal) / 3600) * shopHourlyRateUsd;

const blankAreaM2 =
  (((bbox.widthMm + nestGapMm) * (bbox.heightMm + nestGapMm)) / 1_000_000) *
  (1 + scrapPercent / 100);

const directUnitCostUsd =
  blankAreaM2 * pricePerM2Usd +
  machineCostUsd +
  pierceCount * costPerPierceUsd +
  setupFeeUsd / quantity;

// Round unit price ONCE to integer cents so Unit_Price * Qty === Line_Total to $0.00!
const quotedUnitPriceCents = Math.round(directUnitPriceWithMargin(directUnitCostUsd) * 100);
const quotedLineTotalCents = quotedUnitPriceCents * quantity;

Rounding quotedUnitPriceCents to integer cents before multiplying by quantity guarantees that Unit Price × Qty === Line Total and sum(Lines) + Setup + Tax === Grand Total reconcile to $0.00 across browser tables, client PDFs, and ERP CSVs.

Open-Source Module & Browser Workbench
