  • MIT ES Module & Interactive Spec: github.com/kaiyilu/dxf-laser-quote-math (Live Field Guide) — zero-dependency solvers and node:test suite covering bulge arcs, OCS transforms, 2-core topology, and cent-exact quoting.
  • Browser-Local CAD Quoting Workbench: Laser Cutting Cost Calculator (DXF & SVG) — drop 2D .dxf and .svg files locally in your browser (with $INSUNITS unit confirmation, dark blueprint open-loop inspection, and saved browser shop-rate presets) without uploading customer CAD geometry to a third-party queue.

articles.title: Cube.js : Your SQL Queries Are Secure. But Is Your Cache Leaking Another Tenant's Data?
articles.description: Continuation of this blog : Cube.js + SQL Injection: Just Because It's an Analytics Layer Doesn't...
articles.body_html:
Continuation of this blog : Cube.js + SQL Injection: Just Because It's an Analytics Layer Doesn't Mean Hackers Can't Do Math!

Multi-tenant security doesn't end when your SQL query is safe. Sometimes, the real problem is hiding in your cache.

Imagine this.

You've built a beautiful analytics dashboard using React and Cube.js.

You have:

  • Authentication working.
  • JWT validation in place.
  • Row-level security configured.
  • Tenant-specific filters applied.
  • Database access restricted.

Your security checklist looks green. ✅

You deploy to production, and everything works perfectly.

Until one day, a customer reports:

"Why am I seeing another company's sales figures?"

You investigate the SQL queries. Everything looks correct.

You check the authentication. No issues.

You check the tenant ID. Correct.

Then you discover something interesting.

The database query wasn't the problem. The cached result was.

Welcome to one of the less obvious challenges in multi-tenant analytics: cache isolation.

1. Understanding the multi-tenant problem

Suppose you're building an analytics platform for multiple dealerships.

Each dealership is a tenant.

Let's take two dealerships:

Metric Dealership A Dealership B
Total leads 1,500 850
Converted leads 300 120
Revenue ₹25 lakh ₹12 lakh

Dealership A should never see Dealership B's numbers, and vice versa.

Your application uses Cube.js to process analytical queries.

A simplified architecture looks like this:

       React Dashboard
              |
              v
       Authentication
              |
              v
          Cube.js
              |
       Tenant Security
              |
              v
        Query Engine
              |
              v
       Cache / Pre-aggregations
              |
              v
           Database

Everything looks good.

But there's another question we need to ask:

Does the caching layer understand which tenant owns the data?

2. What happens when caching enters the picture?

Cube.js provides caching and pre-aggregations to improve analytical query performance.

Let's understand the difference.

Query result caching

When an analytical query executes, Cube can cache its result so that equivalent subsequent queries can be served faster.

Pre-aggregations

These are materialized, precomputed query results. Instead of repeatedly aggregating millions of database records, Cube can use an existing pre-aggregation.

For example, imagine calculating daily sales for an entire year.

Instead of repeatedly scanning millions of transactions, Cube can use a pre-aggregated result.

That's great for performance.

But performance optimizations must preserve the same security boundaries as the original query.

3. The cache isolation scenario

Let's walk through a hypothetical misconfiguration.

Both dealerships open the same dashboard.

They select:

  • Date range: Last 30 days
  • Metric: Total sales
  • Region: South

Dealership A opens the dashboard first.

Cube processes the query and caches the result.

First request: Dealership A

Tenant: Dealership A
Dashboard: Sales
Filters: Last 30 days, South

Result: ₹25,00,000

       |
       v

   Cached Result

Now Dealership B opens the same dashboard with identical filters.

If the cache key or pre-aggregation isolation is incorrectly configured and doesn't distinguish the tenant context, the cached result could be reused across tenants.

Potential security failure:

Tenant A requests dashboard
          |
          v
Query executes
          |
          v
Result cached: ₹25,00,000
          |
          |
Tenant B requests same dashboard
          |
          v
Incorrect cache reuse
          |
          v
Tenant B receives ₹25,00,000

Dealership B should have received ₹12,00,000.

This is a hypothetical failure scenario, not the default behaviour of Cube.js.

The important lesson is that tenant context must be preserved across query execution, caching and pre-aggregation selection.

4. Your security context should travel with the query

One important feature of Cube.js is its security context.

Typically, the application authenticates a user and issues a signed JWT containing trusted claims such as:

{
  "user_id": "user_101",
  "tenant_id": "dealership_A",
  "role": "dealer_admin"
}

Cube.js validates the token and uses the security context to enforce data access restrictions.

The key principle:

Never trust a tenant ID simply because it came from the frontend.

A user can modify browser requests.

Instead:

  1. Authenticate the user.
  2. Determine their tenant on the trusted backend.
  3. Issue a signed token containing the tenant identity.
  4. Validate the token in Cube.js.
  5. Apply tenant restrictions through the security context.

For example, a conceptual row-level restriction could look like:

cube(`Orders`, {
  sql: `
    SELECT *
    FROM orders
    WHERE tenant_id = '${SECURITY_CONTEXT.tenantId.value}'
  `
});

This is illustrative rather than a copy-paste configuration. Use Cube's supported security-context and query-rewriting mechanisms for your version, and ensure values are safely handled.

The objective is to make tenant isolation part of the data-access layer, rather than relying on frontend filters.

5. What about pre-aggregations?

This is where things get particularly interesting.

Pre-aggregations are materialized results that Cube can reuse to serve analytical queries.

When building a multi-tenant analytics platform, you need to consider how those pre-aggregations are scoped.

There are different approaches depending on your architecture.

Approach A: Shared pre-aggregations

A shared pre-aggregation can contain data for multiple tenants, provided it retains the tenant dimension and every query is correctly scoped by trusted tenant context.

For example:

daily_sales
--------------------------------
tenant_id | date       | revenue
--------------------------------
A         | 2026-11-01 | 100000
B         | 2026-11-01 | 75000

The tenant restriction must still be enforced when the pre-aggregation is queried.

Approach B: Tenant-specific pre-aggregation schemas

For stronger physical separation, Cube supports configuring the pre-aggregation schema based on the security context.

Conceptually:

preAggregationsSchema: ({ securityContext }) => {
  return `pre_aggregations_${securityContext.tenantId}`;
}

This is a simplified example. In production, validate and sanitize the tenant identifier before using it in a schema name.

This approach can help isolate pre-aggregation storage between tenants, although it introduces additional storage and operational considerations.

The right choice depends on tenant count, data volume, performance requirements and isolation requirements.

Important: Don't assume that manually adding a tenant ID to an arbitrary cache key is the fix. Cube has its own query caching and multi-tenancy mechanisms. Understand how your deployed Cube version incorporates security context into query execution and cache identity before implementing custom cache logic.

6. How do we test for cache leakage?

Here's a practical test worth adding to your multi-tenant application's security testing strategy.

Don't just test whether Tenant A can access its own data.

Test what happens when Tenant A has already populated the cache and Tenant B requests the same dashboard.

The two-tenant test

  1. Login as Tenant A.

Open the dashboard and execute the query.

  1. Populate the cache.

Ensure the query result is cached and the relevant pre-aggregation is available.

  1. Login as Tenant B.

Open the same dashboard with exactly the same filters and date range.

  1. Verify the response.

Confirm that Tenant B receives only its own data.

  1. Reverse the order.

Repeat with Tenant B first and Tenant A second.

Expected result:

Tenant A and Tenant B must always receive their own numbers, regardless of request order or cache state.

Also test:

  • Cold cache versus warm cache.
  • Query result cache versus pre-aggregation hits.
  • Different users within the same tenant.
  • Different tenants using identical query parameters.
  • Cache refresh and pre-aggregation rebuild scenarios.
  • Scheduled reports and exports, not just interactive dashboards.

A successful test with an empty cache isn't enough.

The real test is whether tenant isolation survives when the cache is already populated.

7. Don't forget database permissions

Now let's move one layer deeper.

Suppose your Cube.js service connects to your production database using an account that has full permissions.

It can:

  • Read every table.
  • Insert records.
  • Update customer information.
  • Delete records.

But your analytics dashboard only needs to read sales, leads and dealership information.

Why should it have permission to do anything else?

This is where the principle of least privilege comes in.

Create a dedicated database account for Cube.js.

Permission Recommended access
Read required analytics tables Allowed
Read unrelated sensitive tables Denied
Insert records Denied
Update records Denied
Delete records Denied
Database administration Denied

Even if an application-level security control fails, restricted database permissions reduce the potential impact.

Remember, read-only access does not automatically guarantee tenant isolation. It limits what the service can do, not necessarily which tenant's records it can read.

8. Multi-tenant analytics security checklist

Before deploying a Cube.js application, consider these checks.

Authentication and authorization

  • Validate signed JWTs.
  • Derive tenant identity from trusted claims.
  • Never trust frontend-supplied tenant IDs.
  • Enforce row-level restrictions.

Caching and pre-aggregations

  • Understand how security context affects query cache identity.
  • Verify tenant isolation for shared pre-aggregations.
  • Consider tenant-specific pre-aggregation schemas where appropriate.
  • Test both cold-cache and warm-cache scenarios.
  • Validate isolation across API instances and refresh workers.

Database security

  • Use dedicated database credentials.
  • Prefer read-only access for analytics workloads.
  • Restrict access to required schemas and tables.
  • Avoid unnecessary database privileges.

Testing and monitoring

  • Test with at least two tenants.
  • Test identical dashboard queries across tenants.
  • Test exports and scheduled reports.
  • Monitor unexpected access patterns.

9. Final thoughts

When building multi-tenant applications, we often focus heavily on authentication and SQL query security.

But security doesn't stop when the query is executed.

It continues through caching, pre-aggregations, background refreshes and database permissions.

A secure query with an incorrectly shared cached result can still expose sensitive information.

A read-only database account with unrestricted access to every tenant's data can still create a serious isolation problem.

The goal isn't just to make sure the query is safe.

It's to make sure the entire data journey respects the tenant boundary.

Because in a multi-tenant application, one customer's dashboard should never become another customer's data source.

Let's discuss!

For developers working with Cube.js or other analytics platforms:

  1. Do you prefer shared pre-aggregations or tenant-specific schemas?
  2. How do you test tenant isolation when caching is enabled?
  3. Have you encountered unexpected behaviour with cached analytical results?

I'd love to hear how other teams approach this problem.

Further reading

  • Cube.js Documentation – Pre-Aggregations
  • Cube.js Documentation – Security
  • Cube.js Documentation – Multi-Tenancy

articles.title: Our analytics read zero for a month. Three bugs were hiding in plain sight
articles.description: We shipped three custom metrics to answer one question: how long does a user spend on each tool, and...
articles.body_html:
We shipped three custom metrics to answer one question: how long does a user spend on each tool, and how much do they produce?

seconds. output_kb. A dimension called tool_slug. Two weeks later the GA4 report looked like this:

city event name events seconds output_kb
(not set) — 12 0 0
Rome — 8 0 0
Kuala Lumpur — 6 0 0
Total 59 0 0

59 events. Every custom metric zero. The obvious reading is "we configured something wrong", so I spent the first hour in the GA4 admin UI, re-checking custom definitions, looking for a typo in a parameter name.

The configuration was fine. What was broken was three layers deeper, and each layer looked healthy on its own.

Here is the pipeline, with the three places it broke:

The only method that works: trust the wire

Dashboards lie by omission. A metric showing 0 means "no rows", which is indistinguishable from "no data" and from "no such event". So before touching any config, I asked the browser what it actually sent:

performance.getEntriesByType('resource')
  .map(r => r.name)
  .filter(n => n.includes('/collect'))

That is every GA4 hit the page made — including sendBeacon and fetch requests that the DevTools Network panel shows but that a window.fetch monkey-patch will miss (gtag caches the native reference).

The result:

en=page_view          (no custom parameters)
(no en)               (consent/config ping)

Two requests total. Not one of our custom events. Not tool_view, not file_selected, not process_start, not export_download. The dashboard was not empty because of a config mistake — it was empty because nothing was ever sent.

That reframed the whole problem. The question stopped being "why is the number zero" and became "where do the events die".

Break #1 — the event that never fired

seconds and output_kb were supposed to ride on an event called tool_finish, wired to a window CustomEvent that every export dispatches:

// analytics.ts — fires when any tool produces a file
window.addEventListener('musepdf:download', (event) => {
  track('tool_finish', {
    tool_slug: slug,
    seconds: Math.round((Date.now() - started) / 1000),
    output_kb: Math.round(event.detail.bytes / 1024),
  });
});

tool_finish never appeared in the dataLayer. So I dispatched the event by hand:

window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('musepdf:download', { detail: { bytes: 123456 } }))
// dataLayer: 21 -> 21

Nothing. The listener was never attached — the wiring ran, but the browser's listener registry had no entry for that event type. So the single event carrying both metrics had never fired in production, and no amount of GA4 configuration could have produced a row.

Meanwhile, the events that did fire carried the wrong shape entirely:

process_start     { tool_slug }
process_success   { tool_slug, duration_bucket: "<1s" }
export_download   { tool_slug, output_size_bucket: "<10mb" }

duration_bucket is a string. A GA4 custom metric is numeric. Even if those events had reached the network, "<1s" can never average to a number.

Lesson one: a registered custom metric is not a collected one. GA4 will happily accept a definition for a parameter that no event ever sends. The definition is not the problem; it just reports the absence faithfully.

Break #2 — the queue that stops draining

Fixing the listener was not enough, because the events were also not leaving the page. dataLayer contained all seven events, in both shapes, with Google's own gtm.uniqueEventId stamped on them:

{ event: "export_download", tool_slug: "merge", output_size_bucket: "<10mb", gtm.uniqueEventId: 25 }
["event", "export_download", { tool_slug: "merge", output_size_bucket: "<10mb" }]

So track() worked, dataLayer worked, and window.dataLayer.push was still gtag.js's own hooked function — I checked:

String(window.dataLayer.push).slice(0, 40)
// "function(){var h;ao();if(Zn.H.SANDBOXED_JS_SEMAPHORE>0){h=[];for(var k=0;k<argum"

And yet: no network request.

The decisive experiment was timing. Calling gtag('event', …) by hand:

  • immediately after load → hit sent, en=probe&epn.seconds=7 on the wire;
  • four seconds later → nothing;
  • with consent defaulted to granted up front → still nothing.

So gtag.js on this property drains whatever was queued while it initialised, and then stops reading the array. Every event pushed after that point — which is every real user action, since nobody merges a PDF in the first 500 ms — went into a queue nobody drains.

I could not find the upstream cause with confidence, and I stopped looking once I had a reproducible boundary, because there is a supported answer that does not depend on gtag's internals: send the hit yourself.

Break #3 — the fix that never shipped

Two bugs fixed, bundle deployed, and the metrics were still zero — because returning visitors were running last week's JavaScript.

GET /assets/analytics-v2.js
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
Age: 182168
cf-cache-status: HIT

Age: 182168 — the edge was serving a 50-hour-old copy of a file I had deployed twice since. Same URL, query string or not:

/assets/analytics-v2.js            8781 bytes  (old)
/assets/analytics-v2.js?x=1759...  9113 bytes  (new)

The cause was in public/_headers:

/assets/analytics-v2.js
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate

/assets/*
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

Cloudflare Pages applies every matching rule in order and the last value wins. The wildcard came second, so immutable was what shipped — for a file whose whole purpose is to be updated.

immutable means the browser will not even revalidate for a year. So every analytics fix I had ever shipped was invisible to anyone who had already visited. Add a contradictory must-revalidate and it does not save you: immutable wins.

The fix

Three changes, each addressing one layer, none of them clever:

1. Emit the event where the data is. tool_finish now fires from the export click handler, which already knows the blob size — not from an event listener that may or may not be attached.

const report = (bytes: number, filename: string) => {
  const seconds = Math.max(1, Math.round(performance.now() / 1000));
  const kb = Math.max(1, Math.round(bytes / 1024));

  track('export_download', { tool_slug: slug, seconds, output_kb: kb, /* … */ });
  if (taskFinished) return;          // one finish per page view
  taskFinished = true;
  track('tool_finish', { tool_slug: slug, seconds, output_kb: kb, output_type: type });
};

2. Post the hit directly, in gtag's own encoding. Same endpoint gtag uses, same ep. / epn. convention, cookieless:

function ping(event: string, params: Record<string, unknown>): void {
  const q = new URLSearchParams({ v: '2', tid: measurementId, cid: sessionId(), sid: sessionId(), en: event });
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(params)) {
    if (value === null || value === undefined || value === '') continue;
    q.set(typeof value === 'number' ? `epn.${key}` : `ep.${key}`, String(value));
  }
  navigator.sendBeacon(`https://www.google-analytics.com/g/collect?${q}`);
}

sessionId() lives in sessionStorage only — it dies with the tab, which is exactly what a cookieless ping should do.

3. Version the URL by content. A post-build script hashes the loader and rewrites the reference in every built page:

const hash = createHash('sha256').update(body).digest('hex').slice(0, 10);
html.replace(/\/assets\/(analytics-v\d+\.js)(?!\?)/g, `/assets/$1?v=${hash}`);

A new build is a new cache key. And the specific _headers rule moved below /assets/* so future edits revalidate even if the hash is identical.

Verified end to end on production, on the wire:

en=tool_finish        ep.tool_slug=merge  epn.seconds=6  epn.output_kb=1  ep.output_type=pdf
en=export_download    ep.tool_slug=merge  epn.output_kb=1  epn.seconds=7
en=process_success    ep.tool_slug=merge  ep.duration_bucket=<1s

Six custom events, all six on the wire, plus page_view — seven hits where there used to be one, with exact numbers where exact numbers belong.

A checklist you can run on your own site

  1. Read the wire, not the dashboard. performance.getEntriesByType('resource').filter(n => n.includes('/collect')). A 0 in a report and a missing request are different bugs.
  2. Confirm the event that carries your parameter actually fires. Push to dataLayer and check it appears. If it does not, nothing downstream matters.
  3. Check the shape of your parameters. GA4 metrics are numeric. duration_bucket: "<1s" is a dimension; it will never fill seconds.
  4. Check your assets' cache headers. curl -I https://yoursite/assets/app.js | grep -i cache. If you see immutable with a long max-age on a file you intend to change, every fix you ship is optional for returning visitors.
  5. Do not assume consent mode is the culprit. I did, and it cost a day: granting analytics_storage up front changed nothing.
  6. Watch revokeObjectURL. Unrelated to analytics, but the same debugging session: revoking a blob URL immediately after a.click() can cancel a large download with no error at all. Defer it.

What this cost, and what it bought

The expensive part was not the fix — it was the assumption that a familiar tool (gtag + dataLayer + a track() helper) was doing the obvious thing. Each layer had a plausible excuse, and the dashboard reported all three identically: 0.

The cheap part is now: one function that posts hits, and a build step that guarantees the code actually reaches the browser.

See it working — this is the product the metrics belong to, a client-side PDF toolkit where nothing is uploaded:

40 seconds, no upload: musepdf.app · MP4 · source

articles.title: El fixture sale del código, no al revés
articles.description: Un auditor de flujos de dinero vale lo que vale su entrada. El fixture de este ejemplo se deriva del código con un extractor que falla cerrado: 13 hallazgos antes, 0 después, y mover una guarda del código mueve el grafo.
articles.body_html:
Repositorio: alexisromtz-lab/fsm-ledger-guard @ 2ace0c8 (v0.1.4). Depósito citable: 10.5281/zenodo.24548850. Todas las cifras de este texto salen de corridas reproducibles sobre ese commit; los comandos van al final.

El problema de un auditor es su entrada

Un verificador de máquinas de estados financieras tiene un punto débil que no está
en las reglas: está en el archivo que le das de comer. Si el grafo se transcribe a
mano leyendo el código, el auditor mide la transcripción, no el sistema. Y como la
transcripción la escribe la misma persona que quiere dormir tranquila, el error
siempre cae del lado amable: se olvida la arista que fuga, se anota la guarda que
falta.

El repositorio alexisromtz-lab/fsm-ledger-guard resolvía eso con una promesa y la
promesa no es una medición. La versión 0.1.4 cierra el hueco con una pieza pequeña:
un extractor que lee el código fuente y deriva el grafo, y una compuerta de
deriva que falla si el fixture commiteado deja de ser lo que el código produce.

Qué lee el extractor, y qué se niega a leer

Son 60 líneas de JavaScript repartidas en dos árboles de referencia —pre_fix (32
líneas) y post_fix (28)— y cuatro escrituras de estado en cada uno. El extractor
busca sentencias UPDATE … SET estado = '<literal>', las asocia a la función
nombrada más cercana y lee el WHERE para decidir desde qué estados puede
dispararse esa arista:

  • con guarda (AND estado = 'x' o AND estado IN (…)) la arista tiene un origen declarado y compite por él;
  • sin guarda, la arista sale de todos los estados declarados, incluidos los terminales: que es exactamente lo que hace el SQL sin WHERE de origen.

La semántica de dinero —cuánto mueve cada evento— vive en un archivo declarado,
maquina.json, porque un delta no se deduce del texto de un UPDATE. Todo lo demás
sale del código. Y en las dos direcciones: una escritura sin declaración, o una
declaración sin escritura que la respalde, devuelven NO_MEDIDO con el locus y el
fragmento que no se pudo leer, no un cero silencioso.

Trece y cero, con las reglas a la vista

El mismo motor —once reglas, sin cambios— sobre los dos árboles:

árbol aristas RC hallazgos por regla
pre_fix 12 1 13 FSM001·1, FSM005·4, FSM008·6, FSM010·1, FSM011·1
post_fix 5 0 0 —

En pre_fix el ciclo P2 devuelve +69 900 centavos por vuelta —el precio entero de
un pedido— y las cinco aristas que mueven dinero no declaran clave de idempotencia,
así que el mismo webhook aplicado dos veces mueve el recurso dos veces. La
conservación del saldo abre en profundidad 8 con frontera 4: 30 estados de saldo y 71
aplicaciones sin cierre. En post_fix la frontera es 0 y el espacio se cierra en 5
estados y 5 aplicaciones.

La prueba que casi nadie hace: mover el código y ver si el auditor se entera

Un fixture generado solo se demuestra generado si cambia cuando cambia el código.
Dos mutaciones de un token, en una copia del árbol, sin tocar el fixture commiteado:

mutación aristas deriva RC del auditor hallazgos
añadir AND estado IN ('nuevo') a marcarPagado en pre_fix 12 → 8 DESFASE (RC 1) 1 6
quitarla en post_fix 5 → 9 DESFASE (RC 1) 1 4

Dos cosas que me importan más que el titular.

La primera: quitar una guarda devuelve el verde a rojo sin que nadie edite el
fixture. El paso de RC 0 a RC 1 no lo decidió una persona mirando un diff; lo
decidió el grafo que el código produce hoy, con conservación abierta en 21 saldos y
42 aplicaciones.

La segunda: una guarda no es la cura. Añadir la guarda correcta a una de las
cuatro escrituras baja el conteo de 13 a 6 y el veredicto sigue en RC 1, porque el
ciclo se reconstruye por las otras tres. Si el auditor hubiera sido una heurística
que busca el patrón «SET estado sin WHERE estado», esa mutación lo habría puesto
en verde y el defecto seguiría vivo. La diferencia entre las dos lecturas es la
diferencia entre un lint y un modelo.

Once reglas, cinco flujos, tres sistemas

El mismo motor se corrió sobre dos sistemas privados en producción y sobre el
ejemplo público. Sin una regla nueva entre uno y otro:

sistema qué es actos hallazgos
Studio City reservas con anticipo tres commits, 95ea4a71 → e67b9d5a → 251aaff8 8 → 3 → 1
Moon & Rain e-commerce físico, devoluciones antes y después del parche 3 → 0
ejemplo público pedidos con reembolso pre_fix y post_fix 13 → 0

El uno que queda en Studio City no es un defecto pendiente: es una política. La
cancelación de una reserva pagada devuelve 409 a propósito hasta que exista el
estado reembolsado con su asiento negativo; el auditor lo reporta como recurso
retenido, que es la verdad, y la decisión de tenerlo así está escrita al lado.

Lo que este texto no afirma

El punto ciego, sin adornos. El extractor lee sentencias UPDATE … SET estado en
JavaScript. No lee ORMs, no lee procedimientos almacenados, no lee guardas
construidas en el lenguaje (if (estado !== 'pagado') return), no lee SQL generado
en plantillas y no lee migraciones. Los delta de dinero son una declaración: si el
delta declarado está mal, la auditoría hereda el error y la conservación cierra
sobre una aritmética falsa. Y el ejemplo público mide un flujo pequeño y querido
para el examen, no un sistema en producción: los dos casos con dinero real son
privados y lo que se publica de ellos es el conteo y la huella del grafo, no su
código.

Que el fixture se derive del código no prueba que el motor tenga razón. Prueba que
la entrada no está escrita a mano, que es la mitad del problema y la mitad que casi
nadie audita.

Corre las dos compuertas de deriva del ejemplo público, cambia una
guarda en una copia del árbol y mira cuántas aristas se mueven antes de creerle a
cualquier auditor que te entregue un JSON sin la fuente al lado.

Reproducirlo 

cd fsm-ledger-guard/examples/ecommerce_referencia
python3 extraer.py --arbol pre_fix  --salida ../../tests/fixtures/referencia_publica_pre_fix.json  --check
python3 extraer.py --arbol post_fix --salida ../../tests/fixtures/referencia_publica_post_fix.json --check

cd ../..
PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m fsm_ledger_guard scan tests/fixtures/referencia_publica_pre_fix.json   # RC 1
PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m fsm_ledger_guard scan tests/fixtures/referencia_publica_post_fix.json  # RC 0

articles.title: Generating RFC 5545 .ics Calendar Files in 35 Lines of Zero-Dependency JS (2027 Moon Phases & Kodak's 13-Month Grid)
articles.description: This is Part 6 of the zero-dependency engineering series behind SOL-2027 (Part 1 · Part 2 · Part 3 ·...
articles.body_html:
This is Part 6 of the zero-dependency engineering series behind SOL-2027 (Part 1 · Part 2 · Part 3 · Part 4 · Part 5).

Building an interactive 13-month calendar explorer in the browser solves discovery, yet daily planning still lives inside Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, and Outlook. Readers who discovered their fixed-calendar birthday or looked up the 13 lunar cycles wanted one click to drop every 2027 International Fixed Calendar boundary — especially Month 07: SOL (Jun 18 – Jul 15), December 29 (Year Day), and all 13 UTC New Moons — straight onto their existing schedule.

Rather than pulling a 40 KB npm package like ics or ical-generator into a zero-build static site, we implemented a 35-line RFC 5545 generator in pure Vanilla JavaScript that runs identically in Node.js and the browser (Blob download, zero backend).

1. Why Hand-Rolled .ics Generators Break in Apple & Google Calendar

An iCalendar file looks deceptively simple until strict parsers silently reject it. In practice, three RFC 5545 rules cause almost every homegrown .ics export failure:

  1. Strict CRLF (\r\n) line endings (Section 3.1): Unix \n works in forgiving desktop importers, yet strict validators and mobile iOS share sheets expect \r\n between every content line and trailing newline.
  2. All-day DTEND is exclusive (Section 3.6.1): An all-day event on 2027-06-18 (SOL 1) must declare DTSTART;VALUE=DATE:20270618 and DTEND;VALUE=DATE:20270619 (midnight the following morning). Setting DTSTART and DTEND to the same date causes Google Calendar to ignore or collapse the event, while specifying a 28-day span stretches an unwanted banner across an entire month view. Marking each month's opening day as a clean 1-day milestone (with its 28-day span embedded in SUMMARY) keeps users' calendars readable.
  3. 75-octet line folding & text escaping (Sections 3.1 & 3.3.11): Literal backslashes, commas, and semicolons inside SUMMARY or DESCRIPTION must be escaped (\\, \,, \;), and any line exceeding 75 octets must fold with \r\n (CRLF followed by a single ASCII space).

2. The 35-Line Zero-Dependency RFC 5545 Generator

This exact 35-line JavaScript block mirrors web-app/app.js's canonical IFC_MONTHS and NEW_MOONS_2027 UTC ephemeris brackets (computed via Jean Meeus / PyEphem) and emits 27 compliant VEVENTs: 13 IFC month starts, Year Day on 2027-12-31, and all 13 New Moons of 2027.

const IFC_MONTHS = ['JANUARY','FEBRUARY','MARCH','APRIL','MAY','JUNE','SOL','JULY','AUGUST','SEPTEMBER','OCTOBER','NOVEMBER','DECEMBER'];
const NEW_MOONS_2027 = [
  [1,7,20,25],[2,6,15,57],[3,8,9,30],[4,6,23,52],[5,6,10,59],[6,4,19,41],
  [7,4,3,3],[8,2,10,6],[8,31,17,42],[9,30,2,37],[10,29,13,37],[11,28,3,25],[12,27,20,13]
];
const pad = (n) => String(n).padStart(2, '0');
const ymd = (d) => `${d.getUTCFullYear()}${pad(d.getUTCMonth() + 1)}${pad(d.getUTCDate())}`;
const utcStamp = (d) => `${ymd(d)}T${pad(d.getUTCHours())}${pad(d.getUTCMinutes())}00Z`;
const esc = (s) => s.replace(/[\\,;]/g, (c) => `\\${c}`).replace(/\n/g, '\\n');
const fold75 = (s) => (s.match(/.{1,73}/g) || [s]).join('\r\n ');
function buildSOL2027ICS(now = new Date()) {
  const dtstamp = utcStamp(now), events = [];
  const push = (uid, start, end, sum, desc) => events.push([
    'BEGIN:VEVENT', `UID:${uid}@sol-2027.vercel.app`, `DTSTAMP:${dtstamp}`,
    start, end, `SUMMARY:${esc(sum)}`, `DESCRIPTION:${esc(desc)}`, 'END:VEVENT'
  ].map(fold75).join('\r\n'));
  IFC_MONTHS.forEach((name, i) => {
    const s = new Date(Date.UTC(2027, 0, 1 + i * 28)), e = new Date(Date.UTC(2027, 0, 2 + i * 28));
    const end28 = new Date(Date.UTC(2027, 0, 28 + i * 28));
    const span = `${ymd(s).slice(4,6)}/${ymd(s).slice(6)}-${ymd(end28).slice(4,6)}/${ymd(end28).slice(6)}`;
    push(`ifc-m${pad(i + 1)}-2027`, `DTSTART;VALUE=DATE:${ymd(s)}`, `DTEND;VALUE=DATE:${ymd(e)}`,
      `IFC ${pad(i + 1)}: ${name} 1 (${span})`, `Kodak 13x28 Month ${i + 1}/13 (${name}) - 28 days.`);
  });
  push('ifc-yearday-2027', 'DTSTART;VALUE=DATE:20271231', 'DTEND;VALUE=DATE:20280101',
    'DEC 29: YEAR DAY (Outside 7-Day Week)', 'Day 365/365 of SOL-2027 International Fixed Calendar.');
  NEW_MOONS_2027.forEach(([m, d, h, min], i) => {
    const s = new Date(Date.UTC(2027, m - 1, d, h, min)), e = new Date(s.getTime() + 3600000);
    const ifcM = IFC_MONTHS[Math.floor((s - Date.UTC(2027, 0, 1)) / 86400000 / 28)];
    push(`newmoon-${pad(i + 1)}-2027`, `DTSTART:${utcStamp(s)}`, `DTEND:${utcStamp(e)}`,
      `New Moon #${i + 1}/13 (${ifcM})`, `Exact 2027 UTC New Moon: ${pad(h)}:${pad(min)} UTC inside IFC ${ifcM}.`);
  });
  return ['BEGIN:VCALENDAR', 'VERSION:2.0', 'PRODID:-//SOL-2027//IFC 13-Month Calendar//EN',
    'CALSCALE:GREGORIAN', 'METHOD:PUBLISH', 'X-WR-CALNAME:SOL-2027 (13 Months + 13 Moons)',
    'X-WR-TIMEZONE:UTC', ...events, 'END:VCALENDAR', ''].join('\r\n');
}

3. Subtle RFC 5545 & Date-Math Pitfalls Solved

Avoid line.replace(/(.{1,73})(?=.)/g, ...) When Folding

A classic regex trap when writing a one-line folder is pairing {1,73} with a positive lookahead (?=.): on a short 12-character line like BEGIN:VEVENT, the greedy quantifier backtracks to 11 characters so (?=.) can match the final T, splitting every short keyword into BEGIN:VEVEN\r\n T. Matching non-overlapping chunks with line.match(/.{1,73}/g) avoids backtracking altogether and guarantees every physical line stays strictly <= 74 ASCII bytes (under the 75-octet limit, accounting for the single leading space on continuation lines). If you inject non-ASCII emoji or accented characters into SUMMARY, switch from character regex chunking to TextEncoder UTF-8 byte-boundary slicing so multi-byte sequences never split mid-character.

Deterministic UIDs Prevent Duplicate Imports

Notice each event builds an immutable UID (ifc-m07-2027@sol-2027.vercel.app, newmoon-07-2027@sol-2027.vercel.app, ifc-yearday-2027@sol-2027.vercel.app) rather than calling crypto.randomUUID(). If a user downloads the .ics file twice and re-imports it into Apple Calendar or Outlook, stable UIDs merge and update cleanly instead of creating duplicate lunar markers across every month.

Timed UTC Events vs. All-Day VALUE=DATE Markers

IFC month transitions (SOL 1 on 20270618, YEAR DAY on 20271231) use VALUE=DATE because calendar days belong to the user's local midnight. Astronomical syzygies, however, are exact physical instants: New Moon #7 occurs at 2027-07-04 03:03 UTC, which is 23:03 EDT on July 3 in New York and 11:03 CST on July 4 in Singapore. Encoding DTSTART:20270704T030300Z with a trailing Z lets Google, Apple, and Outlook convert each of the 13 New Moons automatically into the user's local timezone while tagging which IFC month (Math.floor((s - Date.UTC(2027, 0, 1)) / 86400000 / 28)) holds it — proving that every single 2027 IFC month gets one New Moon with zero collisions.

4. Client-Side Browser Download & Node Verification

In the browser, wiring buildSOL2027ICS() to a 1-click button takes eight lines using Blob and URL.createObjectURL with text/calendar;charset=utf-8:

function downloadSOL2027ICS() {
  const blob = new Blob([buildSOL2027ICS()], { type: 'text/calendar;charset=utf-8' });
  const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
  const a = Object.assign(document.createElement('a'), {
    href: url,
    download: 'SOL-2027-Google-Apple-Calendar.ics'
  });
  document.body.appendChild(a);
  a.click();
  a.remove();
  setTimeout(() => URL.revokeObjectURL(url), 1500);
}

Node.js Verification Output

Running buildSOL2027ICS(new Date('2026-11-25T00:00:00Z')) directly in Node produces 6,766 bytes across 225 physical lines (Max line bytes: 68 <= 75, CRLF only: true) and 27 unique VEVENT records matching web-app/app.js:

Event Key UID DTSTART (Verified) SUMMARY
Month 01 Start ifc-m01-2027@... VALUE=DATE:20270101 IFC 01: JANUARY 1 (01/01-01/28)
Month 07 SOL ifc-m07-2027@... VALUE=DATE:20270618 IFC 07: SOL 1 (06/18-07/15)
New Moon #7/13 newmoon-07-2027@... 20270704T030300Z New Moon #7/13 (SOL)
New Moon #9/13 newmoon-09-2027@... 20270831T174200Z New Moon #9/13 (AUGUST)
New Moon #13/13 newmoon-13-2027@... 20271227T201300Z New Moon #13/13 (DECEMBER)
Day 365 Intercalary ifc-yearday-2027@... VALUE=DATE:20271231 DEC 29: YEAR DAY (Outside 7-Day Week)

Explore SOL-2027 & Our New Dedicated Planning Hubs

Download the live 2027 calendar export, test your birthday on Kodak's 13-month grid, or explore workflow-specific guides built around the 28-day model:

  • Live 13-Month Converter & 1-Click .ics Export: https://sol-2027.vercel.app
  • All 13 New Moons of 2027 (Exact UTC Table & Lunar Guide): https://sol-2027.vercel.app/moons
  • 28-Day Infradian Cycle Syncing Calendar Guide: https://sol-2027.vercel.app/cycle-syncing
  • GoodNotes & iPad 14-Page Digital Planner Edition: https://sol-2027.vercel.app/goodnotes
  • Homeschool 13×28 Modulo-7 Math & Astronomy Curriculum: https://sol-2027.vercel.app/homeschool
  • 2027 Holiday Shipping Guide (Dec 12 Print Cutoff & $15 Instant Bundle): https://sol-2027.vercel.app/holiday-deals

What iCalendar parser quirks (TZID, RRULE, or Outlook X-WR-CALNAME ignoring) have bitten your apps when generating .ics feeds?

articles.title: How I Compressed 54 3D Models from 220+ MB Down to 15 MB for a 60fps Three.js Power-Grid Tower Defense
articles.description: Playable Live Demo (100% free, zero download, zero signup): POWER TD: Grid Defense...
articles.body_html:
Playable Live Demo (100% free, zero download, zero signup): POWER TD: Grid Defense (power-td.com/en/) · itch.io HTML5 Build
Full 22-Tower Wiki: Strategy Encyclopedia · Global Daily Challenge: power-td.com/daily

When you build a 3D strategy game solo, pathfinding and simulation logic are rarely what stall the project. You can get flow-field mazing and a real-time electrical grid simulation running in a few late nights. What actually kills momentum is staring at 40 grey placeholder cubes—and sending a playtest link to friends only for them to ask: "Wait, which box is the hydro plant, and why won't this turret fire?"

For POWER TD: Grid Defense (https://power-td.com/en/), a free browser-native Three.js tower defense game combining open-field mazing with live multi-source power grids, I used a 2D-concept → Tripo 3D (H3.1) → headless Blender → Meshopt + WebP pipeline to ship 54 custom 3D assets across 18 handcrafted islands, 22 buildings, and 13 enemy species—while keeping the entire playable web bundle around ~15 MB.

Here is the real production breakdown, including the exact traps I hit when a single 10-gold starter crossbow tower exported at 1.87 million triangles and 60.6 MB.

1. The Game Architecture: Why Mazing + Electrical Grids Need Crisp Silhouettes

In POWER TD, players don't place turrets along fixed tracks. Instead:

  • Freeform Mazing: Cheap 0-watt Bastion Crossbows (10G, with Drag-Paint [M]) double as physical maze walls with live anti-block flow-field pathfinding.
  • Physical Electrical Grid: Seven distinct power plants (Geothermal Steam, Day/Night Solar, River Hydro, Wind Ridges, Nuclear Cooling, Kill-Siphon Dynamo, and v3.0's Fusion Torus Core) project blue power rings. Drop any turret or relay inside a blue ring and catenary power cables auto-string without tedious manual wiring.
  • Real Logistics Trade-Offs: Solar drops at night (and every 28 seconds during binary eclipses on Island 17). Each generator has finite sockets and W/s cable transfer bandwidth, so players buffer spikes with Capacitor Banks, hop oceans with 0%-loss Phase Warp Conduits, and toggle [P] Priority Power (3× weight) on key DPS carries.

At zoomed-out isometric camera angles, every structure is thumb-sized. If a Crossbow, Copper Pylon, and Arc Coil all looked like "generic glowing stone obelisks," the game would be unreadable.

Three Art Hard-Rules Before Generating a Single Mesh

  1. Strict 1×1 tile footprint: Roof overhangs beyond 0.88 tile width trick players into thinking adjacent maze lanes are blocked.
  2. Silhouette-first 2D concepts: Every building started as a numbered 1024×1024 2D ortho-style concept sheet (01–45 + expansion waves) so line weight, brass trim, and stone bases matched as one cohesive family before hitting Image-to-3D.
  3. Separate moving parts at concept time: Never ask an AI 3D generator to fuse spinning wind blades or dangling cables onto a building. Hydro waterwheels (39_hydro_wheel_rotor) and wind rotors (38_wind_rotor) were generated as standalone meshes so Three.js can spin them proportionally to live generator efficiency (0%–185%), while power cables are procedural catenary tubes built at runtime.

2. The 60.6 MB Wake-Up Call (And the Automated 4-Step Pipeline)

When I imported the raw GLB for 01_bastion_crossbow—the cheapest starter wall players spam 30+ times per map—Blender's stats panel read:

  • 1,876,712 triangles
  • 60.60 MB for one single tower (heavier than the entire finished 54-model game!)
  • The stone base and rotating crossbow head were fused into one rigid mesh.

Fixing 50+ models by hand in Blender wasn't an option. Instead, I kept raw exports in a read-only models_raw/ folder (outside Vite's public/ directory) and built a deterministic 4-step pipeline triggered with one npm command (pnpm run normalize-models):

blender --background --python scripts/normalize_models.py
blender --background --python scripts/normalize_env_and_fx_tripo.py
python3 scripts/optimize_glb_textures.py
node scripts/compress_glbs_meshopt.mjs

What Each Stage Actually Does

  1. Footprint Normalization & Pivot Grounding (normalize_models.py):
    • Computes true bounding box, scales every structure proportionally to fit 0.86–0.92 world tiles, grounds bottom vertices cleanly to Y = 0, and auto-decimates extreme outliers (like that 1.87M-tri crossbow) down to strict triangle budgets (<= 16,000 tris for hero buildings, 1,200–6,000 tris for instanced FX/projectiles).
    • Horizontally slices rotating turrets (Crossbow, Mortar, Railgun, Laser) along a clean cut plane into a static base + TurretPivot child group so Three.js can track enemies smoothly without re-rigging.
    • Preserves native skinned skeletal walk clips (e.g., 65-joint rigged crawlers and bosses) while using lightweight procedural hover/pulse animations for hovering enemies.
  2. Texture Downscaling & Delighting (optimize_glb_textures.py):
    • Caps hero buildings & enemies to 1024px PBR maps and small instanced hardware/projectiles to 512px, re-encoding textures as WebP.
    • Using Delighted albedo maps ensures Three.js real-time sun/night lighting and electric arc point-lights look consistent instead of fighting baked studio shadows.
  3. Meshopt Geometry Quantization (compress_glbs_meshopt.mjs):
    • Runs gltfpack / Meshopt compression across every GLB.
    • Example real result on 25_capacitor_bank.glb: 3.91 MB raw → 1.41 MB after 1K texture pass → 0.35 MB after Meshopt + WebP (with zero geometry lost: still exact 13,837 triangles).
    • Across the initial 45-asset library: 222.81 MB raw → 12.16 MB production (~94.5% reduction). Even after expanding to v3.0 Stormfront (54 models, 18 islands, 22 towers, 13 monsters), the entire multi-platform build stays around ~15 MB.

3. Runtime Performance Tricks in Three.js

Keeping download size small is only half the battle—rendering 60+ active towers, glowing power cables, 100+ enemies, and particle bursts at 60fps in a browser tab (including mobile Safari/Chrome) required a few strict guardrails:

  • Zero runtime allocations inside hot loops: Projectiles, floating damage pools, and terrain tile meshes reuse InstancedMesh buffers and pooled DOM nodes (especially critical at 4× combat speed where recreating Live DPS DOM rows detached user clicks).
  • One mesh, three gameplay states: Rather than loading separate models for unpowered/charged/overdriven states, a single Capacitor Bank GLB communicates grid charge via emissive shader uniforms, pulsing cable color, and an adjacent +22%–35% fire-rate aura ring once charge passes 40%.
  • Progressive loading + 2D fallback: Only essential boot models load before frame 1 (loadPolicy.ts + assetQueue.ts); secondary island assets stream in the background. On low-end laptops or mobile data, players can flip to a crisp 2D tactical plane view or cap DPR (1.0× / 1.5× / 2.0×) in one click.
  • Zero-friction sharing via Cloudflare Pages + D1: Every run can export its entire maze + Lv.2 upgrade branches into a compact ?bp=BP1... URL or a /c/<code> challenge card with dynamic Open Graph meta tags, alongside a deterministic Global Daily Challenge (/daily) and a Community Blueprint Wall.

Try It Live (Zero Download, No Signup Wall)

  • Play in Browser (EN): https://power-td.com/en/ (also available in 繁體中文, 日本語, 한국어)
  • Today's Global Daily Challenge: https://power-td.com/daily
  • Full 22-Tower & 8-Synergy Wiki: https://power-td.com/en/guide/
  • Trailers & Press Kit: https://power-td.com/press/

I'd love brutal feedback from fellow Three.js / WebGL devs and TD veterans:

  1. How fast does initial boot + frame rate feel on your GPU/mobile device?
  2. Is the power-grid readability (blue rings, socket caps, night solar dips) intuitive by Wave 3?
  3. What do you think of the mazing vs. electrical logistics trade-off on the harder islands (especially Island 17's 28-second rapid eclipses)?

articles.title: Porting an embroidery file library from Python to TypeScript, byte for byte
articles.description: Machine embroidery has a file format problem. A Brother machine wants PES, a Janome wants JEF, a...
articles.body_html:
Machine embroidery has a file format problem. A Brother machine wants PES, a Janome wants JEF, a commercial Tajima head wants DST, a Pfaff wants VP3, and a Bernina often wants EXP. People buy a design, get the wrong file, and search for "convert DST to PES". Most of the free converters they find upload the file to a server.

We wanted one that never uploads anything, so we ported pystitch, the Python embroidery library behind Ink/Stitch, to TypeScript and ran it in the browser. The result is the Embroidery File Converter, MIT licensed, with the source on GitHub.

Disclosure: we're MavenWright, and we also make a commercial embroidery app (StitchKit). The converter is free, MIT licensed and does not need it.

The interesting part was not the formats themselves. It was making the TypeScript version write the same bytes as the Python one, and finding out how many small Python behaviours that takes.

An embroidery file is a list of needle moves

An embroidery file is not an image. It's an ordered list of moves: stitch here, jump there without stitching, trim the thread, stop for a colour change, end. The machine moves the hoop from point to point. Units are usually 0.1 mm.

DST, the oldest and most widely read format, packs each move into 3 bytes. The x and y offsets are spread across those bytes as flags with weights of ±1, ±3, ±9, ±27 and ±81, a balanced ternary system. This is how the port decodes x:

export function decodeDx(b0: number, b1: number, b2: number): number {
  let x = 0;
  x += getbit(b2, 2) * +81;
  x += getbit(b2, 3) * -81;
  x += getbit(b1, 2) * +27;
  x += getbit(b1, 3) * -27;
  x += getbit(b0, 2) * +9;
  x += getbit(b0, 3) * -9;
  x += getbit(b1, 0) * +3;
  x += getbit(b1, 1) * -3;
  x += getbit(b0, 0) * +1;
  x += getbit(b0, 1) * -1;
  return x;
}

Add up the positive weights and you get 121, so a single DST record can move at most 12.1 mm in each direction. The writer splits anything longer into several records. The y axis is decoded the same way and then flipped. The command lives in the top bits of the third byte: one pattern means "jump", another means "colour change", and 0b11110011 means "end of design".

Before the records there is a 512-byte text header made of lines like LA:design name. That LA: at offset 0 is the closest thing DST has to a magic number. DST stores no thread colours at all. A colour change is just a stop, which is why a DST opens grey in most viewers.

PES, Brother's format, is a wrapper. It starts with #PES and a version, and carries the actual stitches in an embedded PEC block, which uses a fixed table of 64 Brother thread colours. Writing PES therefore means matching every colour in the design to the nearest of those 64.

Why port instead of rewriting

Embroidery formats are full of undocumented details, and pystitch has years of them baked in: header quirks, colour tables, the order things are written in. A clean rewrite would lose that. So we set a strict goal: for the same input, the TypeScript writers produce the same bytes as pystitch, and the readers return the same stitches.

To check it, the repo has a parity harness. It sets up a Python 3.12 virtualenv with pystitch 1.0.1, runs both implementations on the same files, and compares the results byte for byte. Our last full run covered 1,615 design files across all five formats, plus 8,075 files written by our own app: the two implementations read all 9,690 identically and wrote 8,075 of 8,075 byte for byte. A smaller synthetic corpus and its reference outputs are committed to the repo, so the parity tests also run on a machine without Python.

Getting to zero mismatches meant copying Python behaviour that JavaScript doesn't have.

1. Python rounds half to even

Python 3's round() uses banker's rounding: round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4. JavaScript's Math.round(2.5) is 3. pystitch rounds in several places: the centre of a design, colour distances, the per-stitch deltas in EXP and VP3. Each half-unit difference shifts a stitch by 0.1 mm and changes the bytes. The port has a pyRound that rounds half to even:

export function pyRound(v: number): number {
  const f = Math.floor(v);
  const d = v - f;
  if (d < 0.5) return f;
  if (d > 0.5) return f + 1;
  return f % 2 === 0 ? f : f + 1;
}

2. JavaScript has a negative zero

Flipping the y axis in Python is -y, and for y = 0 that's just 0: Python integers have no negative zero. In JavaScript, -0 is a separate value. -0 === 0 is true, but Object.is(-0, 0) is false, and so are deep-equality checks that build on it. The port writes 0 - y instead, with a comment so nobody "simplifies" it back.

3. The order of a Python set

This one took the longest. When pystitch builds the PEC palette for a PES file, it iterates over Python sets of threads. A set has no defined order in the language, but CPython iterates it in the order of its internal hash table, which depends on the hashes, the table size, the probing sequence and when the table resizes. That order decides which palette slot each colour gets, and therefore the bytes of the file.

A JavaScript Set keeps insertion order, so it gives a different palette. The port includes pyset.ts, a small model of how CPython 3.12 inserts into and resizes a set table (linear probing, the perturb shift, resize thresholds), used only where pystitch iterates a set. A test checks it against a real CPython 3.12 interpreter. Because it reimplements CPython behaviour, the repo's NOTICE file carries the Python Software Foundation licence text as well as pystitch's MIT licence.

4. One deliberate difference: randomness

When a design that stores no colours (DST, EXP) is written to a format that needs them, pystitch fills in random colours with random.getrandbits(24). We wanted the same input to always give the same output, so the port uses a fixed list of stand-in colours instead. It's the one documented exception to byte parity, and the README says so.

Detecting a format you can't trust

PES (#PES), VP3 (%vsm%) and most DST files (LA:) can be recognised by their first bytes. EXP has no magic at all, some DST files have no header, and JEF has to be recognised by a consistency check on its header. Worse, a DST or EXP reader will happily "read" almost any file: every 3 bytes decode to some move.

So the detector never trusts the extension alone. A .dst file must also have a body that follows DST's record rules, and a .exp must follow the EXP grammar. Common non-embroidery files (PNG, JPEG, PDF, ZIP, GIF, MP4 and friends) and plain text are rejected by signature first, so a renamed photo gives a clear "this is not an embroidery file" instead of a screen full of random stitches.

Running it in the browser

The library in src/ has no browser or Node dependencies; it works on a Uint8Array:

const bytes = new Uint8Array(await file.arrayBuffer());
const { bytes: dst, warnings, outName } = convert(bytes, file.name, "dst");

The web app around it is a small Vite build. Reading, previewing and converting all happen on the user's device, with no upload and no server-side processing. The Docker image (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64) only serves those static files with nginx, with a default-src 'self' Content-Security-Policy, so it's easy to self-host:

docker run -d -p 8080:8080 mavenwright/embroidery-converter:1.0.0

Before each download the converter lists what the target format can't keep. DST and EXP lose thread colours, VP3 loses stops (the pause for placing appliqué fabric), and JEF can only name hoops up to 200 × 200 mm.

Try it or take it apart

  • Use it in the browser: Embroidery File Converter
  • Read the code, the parity harness and the tests: github.com/mavenwright/embroidery-converter
  • Thanks to the pystitch and Ink/Stitch contributors, whose work this is built on.

If you have an embroidery file the converter reads differently from your machine software, an issue with the file attached is the most useful bug report we can get.

articles.title: How we generate 100,000-line files with exactly the bugs we planted
articles.description: We make Build Failed, a game about the bug that ate your evening. Every level is a code editor with a...
articles.body_html:
We make Build Failed, a game about the bug that ate your evening. Every level is a code editor with a few broken characters hidden in it: a missing semicolon, a ) that became ], a 0 that is secretly the letter O, or a fullwidth ； that looks exactly like ;. You find the line, tap the wrong character, and ship.

👉 Try the web demo (no signup, nothing leaves your browser): https://dawncommitgames.com/demo/

The fun part to build was the code itself. Levels go from 19 lines to 100,000 lines with 500 errors, in five languages, and none of it is stored anywhere. Here's how.

1. Generate clean code first, then break it

Every file starts as clean code built from templates (JS, TS, Python, Java and SQL). Before a single error is planted, the clean output goes through a real parser:

  • JavaScript: acorn
  • TypeScript: the TypeScript parser
  • Python: ast
  • Java: javac

If anything fails to parse, the build stops. That gives us one guarantee we care about: the only bug in a file is the one we put there.

2. Precompute every place an error can go

Each template is cut into small blocks (a function, a config object, a class). For every line of every block we precompute the columns where each error type can be planted: the ; at the end of a statement, the ) of a call, a 0 inside a number, the , between arguments.

That turns "plant 500 errors in a 100,000-line file" into "pick 500 entries from a list", spread out so no two errors are closer than three lines.

3. Never store the file: rebuild it from a seed

A 100,000-line file would be megabytes of text. Instead, the device rebuilds it from a seed and a library of ~2,000 validated blocks. And it doesn't even build all of it: the file is a Proxy that looks like a string[] but makes a line only when the editor asks for it.

const lines = new Proxy([] as string[], {
  get(target, prop, receiver) {
    if (prop === 'length') return length;
    const i = Number(prop);
    if (Number.isInteger(i) && String(i) === prop) {
      return planted.get(i) ?? cleanAt(i); // build the line on demand
    }
    return Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver);
  },
});

The editor only renders what's on screen, so only those lines ever exist as strings.

4. Variety without moving a single column

Rebuilding from the same ~2,000 blocks gets repetitive fast. So each block swaps its nouns: a TicketService becomes a CouponService somewhere else. The catch: every error column was precomputed, so the text can't shift.

The trick is to only swap words of the same length:

const NOUN_GROUPS = [
  ['user', 'item', 'cart', 'post', 'task'],
  ['order', 'token', 'event'],
  ['report', 'coupon', 'review', 'ticket'],
];

ticket ↔ coupon keeps every column where it was, so the precomputed error positions stay valid after the swap.

5. Test the code like a reviewer would

Parsers catch syntax, not sense. A generated sort((a, b) => b.price - a.score) parses fine, but any developer will tell you that's a bug. So we generate every stage in CI and scan for things a reviewer would flag: comparisons between two different fields, duplicate keys, a fetchCoupon() calling /api/tickets/. If the scan finds one, the build fails.

What the game looks like

Besides the bug hunts, there's a 100-week "dev career" mode: standups, tickets, a PM who messages you at 11pm, promotions, and a lot of endings (not all of them good). The web demo has stages 1–20 and a 12-week career.

  • 🕹️ Web demo: https://dawncommitgames.com/demo/
  • 📱 Full game (iOS / Android, free): https://dawncommitgames.com/

I'd love to hear which level got you, or how you'd generate "realistic" broken code. Questions about the generator are very welcome in the comments.
